documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping agricultural education globally, but its integration in Nigeria remains in its early stages. This chapter focuses on systematically embedding AI into Nigeria’s agricultural education through pedagogical innovation, institutional readiness, and skills development. Instead of broadly surveying AI’s role, it critically analyzes the necessary frameworks, practices, and policies for its operational inclusion in agricultural training and research. Drawing from empirical evidence and global models (India, Kenya, Brazil, and China), the chapter explores AI-enhanced pedagogies, such as smart learning environments and digital simulations, to bolster competencies in precision agriculture, climate-smart farming, and agribusiness management. The analysis identifies four key dimensions for AI integration: curriculum redesign for competency-based learning; institutional capacity and infrastructure; ethical governance of digital systems; and alignment with Nigeria’s Digital Economy and AI Strategies. While awareness and pilot initiatives are on the rise, challenges like weak infrastructure, limited staff training, and fragmented policy implementation restrict large-scale adoption. The chapter proposes a phased integration model—encompassing awareness, capacity building, curriculum reform, and adaptive feedback—to facilitate sustainable transformation. Ultimately, it argues that AI should be regarded not just as a technological innovation but as a pedagogical framework vital for transforming Nigeria’s agricultural education ecosystem. By aligning AI with national sustainability goals, Nigeria can develop a new generation of digitally skilled, sustainability-focused agricultural professionals prepared for the challenges of the twenty-first-century food system.

Purpose This study presents an integrated systematic mapping of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in construction management, clarifying technique-domain pairings, data and validation practices, and deployment readiness across the construction lifecycle, addressing fragmentation in prior reviews. Design/methodology/approach Following the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidance for study identification and screening and the structured literature review approach, 148 peer-reviewed articles published between 2007 and 2025 across 14 journals were analyzed through bibliometric and thematic synthesis. An open companion web application (https://cm.electriai.com/) was developed, providing bibliometric visualizations, a searchable paper database, and a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) AI assistant. Findings The review shows that AI research in construction management accelerated after 2022 but remains uneven in its technical and methodological development. Technique-domain mapping revealed lock-in patterns: vision-based deep learning (DL) was concentrated in safety, and traditional machine learning (ML) in cost estimation, while optimization, graph neural networks (GNNs), and generative AI remained underexplored. Data constraints persist: 40.5% of studies used datasets below 500 samples, 65.5% relied on private or unreported data, cross-project validation appeared in 1.4% of papers, and explainable AI (XAI) appeared in 3.4%. Practical implications Construction stakeholders require coordinated investment in open benchmark datasets, cross-project validation protocols, XAI integration and interoperable standards for building information modeling and Internet of Things systems. Originality/value This review integrates AI techniques, construction domains, data and validation practices, supported by an open companion web application for verifying, filtering, and querying the evidence base.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping healthcare and organizational management worldwide, yet its benefits remain unevenly distributed between high-income and low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). This review examines the structural drivers of this global AI divide, situates Pakistan's healthcare and digital infrastructure challenges within this context, and presents an institutional case study of four AI-enabled interventions implemented at the Sindh Integrated Emergency and Health Services (SIEHS), an emergency and health services organization under the Health Department, Government of Sindh, Pakistan: an AI-driven recruitment and candidate-job matching system (Talent Match Live), a facial-recognition and geolocation-based field monitoring application, an AI-assisted CCTV training-monitoring system, and an AI-augmented telemedicine triage service embedded within SIEHS's Teletabeeb telehealth department. Each intervention is evaluated against comparable systems documented in the international literature to assess feasibility, evidence of effectiveness, and associated ethical risks. A responsible-adoption framework is proposed to guide organizations in resource-constrained settings toward AI integration that is effective, equitable, and ethically governed. The review concludes that while AI offers meaningful efficiency and access gains for LMIC public-sector organizations such as SIEHS, sustainable adoption requires deliberate attention to data protection, algorithmic bias, workforce consent, and alignment with international ethical guidance.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence implementation in the education field provides revolutionary methods to achieve Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4): ensuring inclusive and equitable quality education and lifelong learning skills acquisition. This chapter assesses the strategic role of the integration of AI in the enhancement of the quality and efficiency of the post-primary education sectors. Through the adoption of the mixed research method that implies the analysis of the literature reviews and case studies, the study investigates the strategic role of AI technologies towards improved teaching practices and the effectiveness of the institutions. This study reveals the potential strategic role that AI technologies can play in reducing the gap in education access and the effective acquisition and implementation of information-based decisions in post-primary educational sectors. Through the strategic adoption of AI technologies, the study reveals the continued challenges posed by ethical approaches towards the adoption of the technologies and the implementation of equity towards capacity building. This study has proved that the adoption of AI technology in post-primary educational sectors can be an effective strategic mechanism towards the goal of SDG 4. This article Presents Recommendations on How Some of the Players Should Incorporate the AI Technologies Offered in the Enhancements of the Educational Processes Towards the SDG 4 Goals.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Middle and secondary school educators should utilize and implement Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a support tool for instruction, not a replacement for their pedagogy and lesson planning. Utilizing and implementing AI can assist with lesson planning, differentiation, feedback, and generating learning materials; and its uses should be guided by clear expectations, professional judgment, and school policy. Educators should also teach their students how to use AI ethically, verify outputs for accuracy and bias, and protect student privacy by avoiding sensitive data. Most importantly, assessments should be designed to show genuine student understanding, with AI used transparently and appropriately. The best available published advice concurs that the usage of AI within an educator’s pedagogy significantly enhances middle and secondary school students’ learning. This article offers practical guidance for educators who use or plan to use AI in the classroom, while also highlighting policy recommendations to support effective educational practices.

documents.abstract: Abstract Machine learning has moved from proof of concept to routine operation in pharmaceutical quality control, yet the autonomy it is granted narrows sharply as products approach release. In this narrative review, we propose that this unevenness reflects not model capability but the regulatory burden an output must clear before it can be acted on, a pattern we term the validation‐barrier gradient. We score this barrier across four stages on criteria covering decision criticality under good manufacturing practice, validation and data‐integrity load, locus of legal liability, and patient‐safety consequence. The composite barrier rises as observed autonomy falls. At final product inspection, deep vision systems already detect defects at line speed, often on small single‐site datasets, but the authority to release a batch still rests with a qualified person. This gap between what a model can do and what it is allowed to decide cannot be explained by task difficulty alone. Closing it requires not further accuracy gains but shared benchmarks, routine robustness reporting, and change‐control pathways allowing validated models to be updated rather than frozen.

documents.abstract: Abstract This study examines teachers’ perceptions of and orientations to Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the context of Religious Education (RE), drawing on survey data collected from 54 in-service RE teachers participating in the SUB8 professional development programme in Greece. Using a descriptive survey design grounded in the frameworks of Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK), Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK), AI literacy, and digital self-efficacy, the study maps teachers’ reported practices, competencies, and concerns across seven thematic dimensions. Findings indicate generally positive orientations towards AI-assisted instructional design within this cohort, alongside significant theological and pedagogical concerns regarding its use in spiritually sensitive contexts. Qualitative responses point to three recurring themes: the productive utility of AI for lesson preparation and differentiation; persistent concerns about accuracy, depth, and the reliability of AI-generated content; and a strong consensus that AI must function as a supplementary pedagogical tool, subordinate to the relational and experiential dimensions of RE. Because participants were self-selected members of an AI-focused training programme and were surveyed immediately upon its completion, these findings are interpreted as descriptive of this specific professional development context rather than of Greek RE teachers in general. The study complements recent comparative evidence from Germany and Poland by providing, to the author’s knowledge, the first empirical account of AI perceptions among RE teachers within an Orthodox national professional development context, and it foregrounds a theological and epistemological dimension still largely absent from AI-in-education research.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to source applicants, display screening packages, match candidates, communicate with applicants, and analyse workforce data. Processing speed alone does not indicate whether it is AI-powered. Recruitment outcomes also include shortlist relevance, applicant delight, recruiter productivity, and high-quality decisions. This study examines the relationship between AI adoption and five perceived skill-acquisition outcomes, drawing on questionnaire responses from 70 individuals. The analysis uses descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation, and separate simple linear regression. AI adoption undoubtedly improves recruitment performance (β = 0.546, R2 = 0.282), recruitment effectiveness (β = 0.514, R2 = 0.295), perceived candidate experience (β = 0.569, R2 = 0.363), recruiter productivity (β = 0.498, R2 = 0.329) and overall performance of talent acquisition (β = 0.341, R2 = 0.120). All five regression relationships are statistically significant at the 5% level. Candidate experience has the highest R2 among the five factors, while specific skill acquisition performance has the lowest. Additionally, respondents who report greater AI adoption tend to report more favourable recruiting outcomes, but the study does not establish causality or confirm changes in overall objective hiring performance. The article discusses these findings in relation to fairness, transparency, confidentiality, and human oversight. It recommends that firms assess the use of multiple end-result markers in AI-enabled hiring and conduct meaningful human assessment of the resulting options.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence (AI) integration, management effectiveness, and school–enterprise collaborative talent training at Guangzhou Huali Vocational College of Science and Technology, China. A descriptive-correlational quantitative design involved 159 students and 101 teachers during the second semester of academic year 2025–2026. Students were included through total enumeration and teachers through purposive sampling. A researcher-developed questionnaire was validated by five experts and pilot-tested with 30 individuals; Cronbach’s alpha was 0.96. Analysis used frequencies, percentages, weighted means, t tests, one-way analysis of variance, and Pearson correlations. Both groups rated AI integration as high, management effectiveness to a high extent, and training success to a high degree. Students’ assessments differed significantly by enterprise exposure across all three constructs; teachers’ AI integration assessments differed by position. AI integration correlated positively with management effectiveness for students (r = 0.8839) and teachers (r = 0.9225). Management effectiveness correlated positively with training success for students (r = 0.9399) and teachers (r = 0.9586). The findings support coordinated curriculum, assessment, supervision, faculty development, and workplace learning. A Comprehensive AI Integration Framework was proposed to strengthen institutional practices and collaborative training. The relationships indicate association rather than causation.

Objective To investigate the current status and related factors of innovative behavior among clinical nurses in tertiary hospitals and explore the relationships and pathways among artificial intelligence literacy, AI self-efficacy, organizational innovation climate, and nurse innovative behavior, for providing a basis for targeted nursing management strategies. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted on 850 nurses from six tertiary medical institutions using a stratified survey approach in Yueyang city, Hunan province, from June to July 2026, in the General Information Questionnaire, Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale, Organizational Innovation Climate Scale, and Nurse Innovative Behavior Scale were used. AMOS 24.0 was used to conduct confirmatory factor analysis to assess the model fit of the scales. SPSS 26.0 was used for descriptive statistics, univariate analysis, Pearson correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression. PROCESS macro version 4.2 Models 4 and 14 tested mediation and moderated mediation effects. Results A total of 850 valid questionnaires were obtained, with a valid questionnaire rate of 95.3%. The mean nurse innovative behavior score was 37.93±6.50. The measurement model for the four scales showed good fit, and the scales demonstrated good convergent validity and some evidence of discriminant validity. Artificial intelligence literacy, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, organizational innovation climate, and innovative behavior showed positive associations with one another (r = 0.609–0.797, P < 0.01). Educational level, professional title, participation in research or innovation activities, artificial intelligence literacy, artificial intelligence self-efficacy, and organizational innovation climate were factors associated with nurse innovative behavior and explained 60.9% of the total variance. Artificial intelligence self-efficacy partially mediated the relationship between artificial intelligence literacy and nurse innovative behavior. The indirect effect was 0.322, with a 95% CI of 0.243–0.403, accounting for 52.90% of the total effect. Organizational innovation climate moderated the relationship between artificial intelligence self-efficacy and nurse innovative behavior (b = 0.051, P < 0.01). The index of moderated mediation was 0.041, with a 95% CI of 0.009–0.078. Conclusion AI literacy was closely related to nurse innovative behavior, with AI self-efficacy as a partial mediator and organizational innovation climate as a moderator. Nursing management may focus on AI competencies, application confidence, and organizational support.

AI will emerge as a significant force behind administrative change, although public organisations vary in their preparedness to do so. This paper investigates the impact of digital leadership and employee AI ability on artificial intelligence preparedness and innovation in services in the Bangladesh public administration. A four-reflective construct survey model was created, including digital leadership, employee AI capability, AI readiness, and service innovation. It was analysed with a synthetic dataset of 835 cases that are intended to test the methodology and prove PLS-SEM. The data were evaluated using descriptive statistics, common method bias tests, evaluation of the measurement model, structural model, mediation, and predictive assessment. The findings revealed that the positive impacts of digital leadership and employee AI capability on AI preparedness were significant. Service innovation was also positively impacted by AI readiness significantly. Digital leadership and employee AI capability had a direct impact on service innovation. Both relationships were partially mediated by AI readiness. The model explained 45.4% of the variance in AI readiness and 41.0% of the variance in service innovation. All the predictive relevance values were positive and the PLS model yielded lower prediction errors than linear benchmark. The results reveal a readiness pathway that is coherent where leadership, employee capability, and institutional preparedness contribute to innovation in the delivery of public services.

Background Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are widely used by medical students, but associations of general use frequency and AI-related attitudes with psychological distress remain unclear. Methods All 1,275 active students at one Turkish medical faculty were invited to an anonymous online survey conducted from 1 April to 1 May 2026; 249 of 251 respondents consented. Measures included general AI use, an investigator-translated 13-item Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale (ATAI), and the validated Turkish Depression Anxiety Stress Scales-21. A general-distress composite was the primary outcome, and hierarchical regression used HC3 robust standard errors. Results AI use was reported by 95.6% of participants, and 50.2% reported daily use. Mean doubled DASS-21 total was 56.97 (SD 31.55). The ATAI three-factor model showed mixed fit (CFI = .898, TLI = .872, RMSEA = .107, SRMR = .070). AI-frequency categories did not improve the adjusted model at the block level (change in R -squared = .016, p = .111; robust global p = .088). Adding exploratory ATAI factors increased R-squared by.052 ( p = .002; robust global p = .009); Benefit was inversely, and Risk and Use positively, associated with distress. Subscale sensitivity analyses preserved coefficient directions, but only the inverse Benefit-Anxiety association survived correction across 15 additional focal tests ( q = .032). Conclusion AI use was nearly universal and served both educational and personal/non-educational purposes, but this sample did not provide stable evidence of an overall association between general use frequency and distress. ATAI associations are exploratory and may reflect measurement or common-method processes. Longitudinal multicenter studies should use formally adapted measures and objective indicators of AI engagement.

Background: Cancer screening plays a crucial role in early diagnosis and improved survival, yet conventional screening methods are limited by false-positive findings, false-negative results, interobserver variability, delayed reporting, and unequal access to expert interpretation.Objective: To review recent advances in artificial intelligence-assisted cancer screening, focusing on applications in radiology, histopathology, and liquid biopsy.Methodology: This narrative review summarized published evidence on the role of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning in cancer screening.The review focused on three major domains: AI-assisted radiology, AI-assisted histopathology, and AI-assisted liquid biopsy.Results: AI-assisted radiology has shown value in lesion detection, image classification, risk stratification, and workflow prioritization, particularly in breast and lung cancer screening.In histopathology, AI supports tumor detection, grading, biomarker quantification, margin assessment, and reduction of interobserver variability.In liquid biopsy, AI improves interpretation of circulating tumor DNA, circulating tumor cells, methylation markers, microRNAs, and other molecular biomarkers for early cancer detection and tumor-origin prediction.Conclusion: Artificial intelligence has considerable potential to strengthen cancer screening by improving early detection, diagnostic accuracy, efficiency, and individualized risk assessment.

documents.abstract: Drug delivery research is increasingly influenced by artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, generative AI and large language models (LLMs).These technologies can support pharmaceutical research as well as scientific writing, but the language used to describe formulations, delivery mechanisms and outcomes must remain technically precise.This study evaluates whether controlled AI-assisted linguistic revision can improve the clarity, grammar, readability and terminology consistency of drug-delivery scientific texts while preserving their technical meaning.A comparative pre-edit/post-edit corpus design is proposed in which drug-delivery scientific passages are assessed before and after controlled AI-assisted revision.Human/domain-expert review is used to evaluate linguistic quality and technical meaning preservation.The study framework measures grammar, terminology consistency, clarity, readability, technical meaning preservation and newly introduced technical errors.The final numerical results must be obtained from the completed corpus and scoring process.AI-assisted language technologies may serve as editorial support in drug-delivery research when their outputs are systematically verified by domain experts.The framework distinguishes language enhancement from scientific validation and provides a reproducible interdisciplinary approach to AI-assisted pharmaceutical communication.

Human behavior remains one of the most persistent contributors to cybersecurity incidents, as unintentional errors, social-engineering susceptibility, and insider misuse continue to bypass purely technical safeguards. This conceptual, literature-based study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) techniques can be applied to analyze human behavioral patterns in order to reduce cybersecurity risk and human error within organizational information systems. Drawing on a structured review of insider-threat detection, phishing and social-engineering research, security-awareness training studies, and explainable-AI literature, the study synthesizes recurring behavioral indicators, modeling approaches, and evaluation practices reported across the field. A conceptual AI-based human-behavior-analysis framework is proposed, comprising data acquisition, behavioral feature engineering, AI/ML modeling, explainable risk scoring, and adaptive human-in-the-loop response. The review indicates that sequence-aware deep-learning models, such as long short-term memory networks and autoencoders, combined with explainable AI techniques, achieve strong reported detection performance while preserving analyst interpretability, and that adaptive, behavior-based training interventions are associated with measurably greater reductions in human-related risk than static, one-time awareness programs. The study concludes that integrating continuous behavioral analytics with human-centered training and feedback mechanisms offers a more resilient approach to cybersecurity risk management than technology-only or training-only strategies. Implications for organizational security governance, model interpretability, and future empirical validation are discussed.

Learners often spend a great deal of time condensing lecture slides, textbook chapters and research papers into brief revision notes. Large language models (LLMs) from the generative AI family can draft such notes within seconds, but a model that is not grounded in a source may write confident text that the material never states. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lowers this risk by supplying the model with passages fetched from the learner’s own documents. This paper offers a focused narrative review of verified literature on AI-driven study notes generation with generative AI and RAG. Three linked areas are covered: retrieval and RAG techniques (chunking, dense embeddings, retrievers and advanced pipelines); generative models and prompting (LLMs, structured prompt frameworks and hallucination); and empirical evidence on generative AI in engineering and computing courses. The reviewed work indicates that RAG was proposed to anchor generation in retrieved text, that dense retrieval outperformed a strong sparse baseline in open-domain question answering, and that in a quasi-experiment with 26 students, structured prompts produced fuller answers than free-style prompts. Even so, most educational studies capture student perceptions instead of learning outcomes, rely on small samples, and none of the reviewed studies directly measures note quality, faithfulness or retention. The paper contributes a comparison of representative studies, a conceptual seven-layer architecture that links ingestion, retrieval, grounded generation, verification and learner feedback, and a ranked list of research gaps.

documents.abstract: Bone fractures are among the most common musculoskeletal injuries, and their outcome depends on accurate classification, timely localisation and early recognition of failed healing. Manual radiograph interpretation is subjective and time-consuming, and plain X-ray is slow to reveal healing failure (nonunion), which affects up to 12 % of tibial fractures and can take more than six months to diagnose [1]. Artificial intelligence (AI), combined with medical imaging and novel sensing, is increasingly proposed as a route to fast, consistent and early fracture assessment. This paper presents a focused narrative review of four verified peer-reviewed IEEE Access studies (2022–2025) covering contactless antenna-based sensing of implant deflection and fracture stiffness, X-ray fracture-type classification with transfer learning and ensemble classifiers, two-stage CT-based cervical spine fracture classification and vertebra detection, and attention-enhanced YOLOv8 detection of paediatric wrist fractures. The review examines three connected themes: imaging and sensing technologies (X-ray, computed tomography and near-field electromagnetic sensing), learning methods (CNN transfer learning, hybrid CNN–classical ensembles and object detectors), and clinical integration with explainability. The literature shows that deep models can classify fracture types with about 95–98 % accuracy, that YOLOv8 variants reach about 93.5 % mAP50 for vertebra detection and 65.8 % mAP50 over all wrist-trauma categories, and that a miniaturised Vivaldi antenna (36 × 30 mm) can track sub-millimetre implant displacement. However, most studies use single-source datasets, small test sets, random data splits and offline evaluation, and few report clinical validation. The review contributes a comparative analysis of representative studies, a proposed conceptual architecture linking acquisition, AI inference, decision support and clinical reference validation, and a prioritised agenda of research gaps and future directions.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Milk is a highly perishable, high-value food whose quality is affected by natural compositional variation, economically motivated adulteration with water, sugars, starch, urea or melamine, microbial spoilage during storage and transport, and udder diseases such as mastitis. Reference methods, including laboratory Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) analysis, microbiological culture and chromatography, are accurate but centralised, slow and costly, which restricts routine testing at farm and collection-centre level. Artificial intelligence (AI), combined with rapid sensing and the Internet of Things (IoT), is increasingly proposed as a route to fast, on-site and continuous milk quality assessment. This paper presents a focused narrative review of verified peer-reviewed studies, prioritising 2022–2026 publications, that use AI for milk composition prediction, adulteration detection, spoilage assessment and udder-health prediction. The review examines three connected themes: sensing technologies (mid-infrared, near-infrared and fluorescence spectroscopy, low-cost multispectral chips, electronic noses and smartphone-based vibration sensing), learning methods (partial least squares chemometrics, classical machine learning such as support vector machines, random forests and gradient boosting, and deep learning such as convolutional neural networks), and IoT architectures with edge and cloud inference. The literature shows that spectroscopic data with machine learning or deep learning can detect single adulterants with reported accuracies of about 95–100 %, and that inexpensive 18channel spectral sensors calibrated against laboratory FTIR can estimate fat and protein with mean errors of about 0.07–0.14 %. Simple, interpretable models often perform as well as complex ones. However, most studies use small, single-region datasets, laboratory conditions, single adulterants and random data splits, and few report field validation, sensor drift, uncertainty or long-term IoT operation. The review contributes a comparative analysis of representative studies, a proposed conceptual farmto-plant architecture that links multi-sensor acquisition, edge AI, IoT decision support and laboratory reference validation, and a prioritised agenda of research gaps and future directions.
topics: Milk Quality and Mastitis in Dairy Cows
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid ubiquity of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally disrupted traditional pedagogical frameworks in engineering education, necessitating a critical examination of its impact on cognitive development and knowledge retention. This longitudinal study spans 30 years (1996–2025) to analyse shifts in student learning curves within an AI curriculum, testing the hypothesis that reliance on automated tools exacerbates a ‘J-curve’ learning style, characterised by delayed engagement and terminal production spikes, at the expense of fundamental understanding. By comparing weekly topic acquisition and final assessment data across cohorts, the research reveals a distinct morphological transformation from the classic sigmoidal progression (‘S-curve’) of the baseline 1996 class to an exponential ‘J-curve’ in the 2025 cohort. While modern students demonstrate high procedural efficiency in project delivery, this shift correlates strongly with a significant decline in independent examination performance, where mean scores fell from 9.50 to 7.75. Although a gradual decline in performance was observed prior to 2020, the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the subsequent ubiquity of generative AI tools may have intensified this trend (main finding). The data indicate that students utilise AI to bypass the cognitive friction necessary for deep learning, resulting in a failure to exit the assisted phase of skill acquisition. These findings suggest that current AI integration acts as a mechanism for cognitive offloading rather than scaffolding, creating a trade-off between immediate output and long-term declarative competence. The study concludes that engineering curricula must rigorously re-evaluate assessment strategies to ensure that the efficiency of automated generation does not erode the foundational logic required for sustainable innovation.

documents.abstract: This study assesses whether existing intelligent transportation system (ITS) data can be reused for autonomous-driving artificial intelligence (AI) based on task-specific information requirements and the recoverability of missing information. A task-specific framework was applied to five heterogeneous ITS data assets—roadside closed-circuit television (CCTV), camera-based and radar-based automatic incident detection system (AIDS) data, radar-based smart intersection system (SIS) data, and vehicle detection system (VDS) performance-evaluation data—across four data-use tasks: 2D road-user detection training, detection/measurement output validation, event/structured traffic-state retrieval, and road-referenced trajectory reconstruction. For each asset–task pair, mandatory information requirements were identified and classified as explicitly available, directly derivable or linkable, recoverable through feasible transformation, not reliably recoverable, or unconfirmed; these information-level states were then translated into task-specific usability. The results showed that usability varied substantially by task. Camera-based AIDS provided the broadest direct usability, whereas roadside CCTV showed greater reuse potential through transformation. Radar-based AIDS, radar-based SIS, and VDS performance-evaluation data were directly usable for validation and structured traffic-state retrieval, while visual-training and trajectory-reconstruction usability was more limited. Performance-evaluation records showed particular value for validation because they preserved target outputs, validated reference information, and their correspondence. These findings demonstrate that the reuse value of existing ITS data depends on the information actually retained and its recoverability rather than on sensing modality alone. By identifying reusable data and selective future-retention needs, the framework supports more resource-efficient management of digital ITS assets and links task-specific data reuse to sustainable transportation.

Background/Objectives: Saudi Health consumers increasingly rely on generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) to access health information from a growing number of health-related resources. Little is known about the frequency and patterns of generative AI tool use for seeking health information among consumers, its reported impact, and health consumers’ perceptions of these tools. This study aims to investigate the use of and perspectives on generative AI tools among health consumers in Saudi Arabia (SA). It also aims to assess the impact of their use on health-seeking behaviours. Methods: An exploratory, cross-sectional, self-administered online survey was distributed to adults (≥18 years) residing in SA during two data collection rounds in 2026 (March–April and July–August). All adults who used generative AI tools to seek online health information in the past year were included. Bivariate and multivariate analyses were conducted to examine relationships among variables. Results: A total of 403 eligible health consumers (58% male) participated. Among respondents who had used generative AI for health purposes, approximately 49% reported using it more than five times per month. Younger age, higher income, and more frequent pre-use were associated with higher odds of frequent seeking health information behaviour. Headache, abdominal pain, and musculoskeletal pain were the most common claims. ChatGPT was the main platform (84%) used for seeking information. Age was significantly negatively associated with frequency, whereas income and pre-visit use were positively associated. The primary reasons for seeking health information via generative AI were quick information retrieval (71%), time saving (34%), and curiosity (30.5%). Conclusions: The high frequency of use suggests that generative AI can serve as a source of health information and may lead users to withhold health information from healthcare providers. It may influence subsequent health-seeking behaviours, such as requesting urgent care or postponing physician visits. These self-reported findings do not establish diagnostic accuracy, clinical effectiveness, or patient safety, and the clinical risk and appropriateness of self-management actions were not assessed. Many respondents reported concerns about inaccurate information, missed serious illness, and increased health anxiety.

documents.abstract: Abstract Objective This retrospective cohort study evaluated the effect of an artificial intelligence (AI) scribe on patient instructions documentation in ambulatory internal medicine settings. Materials and Methods We analyzed 391 061 adult encounters at a single medical center from December 2023 to July 2025. A difference-in-differences analysis estimated the relationship of AI scribe availability with patient instructions documentation frequency. Mixed-effects logistic regression estimated the association between encounter-level AI scribe utilization and documentation, adjusted for patient, clinician, and encounter characteristics. Length and readability were compared across instructions created by AI alone, clinicians assisted by AI, and clinicians alone. Character-level edit distances between AI drafts and final documentation were calculated. Results AI scribe availability was associated with a 10.5 percentage-point increase in patient instructions documentation frequency (P = .018), and encounter-level AI use was associated with higher odds of documentation (aOR 4.32; 95% CI, 4.14-4.50). AI instructions were longer than clinician-authored content (median 1994 vs 482 characters) and scored higher on 3 text-complexity indices (all P < .001). Clinician editing of AI content increased length without meaningfully reducing complexity. AI drafts and final documentation differed substantially, with a median character-level edit distance of 39.7%. Discussion AI scribe availability was associated with increased patient instructions documentation. However, AI-generated instructions were longer and scored as more linguistically complex than clinician-authored instructions, and clinician editing did not close this gap. Conclusion Ambient AI scribes can improve availability but may increase complexity of patient instructions. Research into downstream effects including patient comprehension and satisfaction is warranted.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) provides opportunities for computational athlete monitoring, adaptive training analysis, and injury-risk modelling. This study presents Athlete-AI, a multimodal AI framework that integrates wearable sensor data, human motion information, pose features, and literature-derived athlete variables into a unified computational architecture. The framework combines multimodal feature fusion, reinforcement learning for adaptive training simulation, and machine-learning-based injury-risk modelling. The evaluation was conducted using publicly available benchmark datasets, including PAMAP2, Human3.6 M, and Microsoft COCO, together with literature-derived parameters used to construct simulated athlete profiles, workload, fatigue, recovery, and injury-risk scenarios. The framework was evaluated through computational experiments and simulation-based athlete-monitoring scenarios to examine multimodal integration, injury-risk classification, and adaptive training behaviour. Repeated-run evaluation across five random seeds, probability-calibration analysis, component ablation, comparison with multimodal fusion baselines, and a leakage-controlled analysis of the dependence on label-defining variables were also performed. When the workload, fatigue, recovery, and biomechanical-risk variables used to define the simulated labels were removed from the predictors, the F1-score decreased from 86.6 to 72.8%. Negative-control analyses showed that the benchmark-derived features-only model produced performance comparable to the shuffled-label control. The results demonstrate the computational feasibility of integrating heterogeneous athlete data and evaluating adaptive training and injury-risk modelling within a unified simulation environment. The reported performance values represent preliminary computational results and do not constitute real-world, clinical, or prospective athlete validation. Therefore, the proposed framework should be regarded as a computational research framework that requires validation with longitudinal data from real athletes before practical or clinical deployment.

documents.abstract: AI agents can now search literature, generate hypotheses, analyze datasets, and run experiments at a scale difficult for researchers to match. Yet scaling scientific execution does not automatically scale researchers' ability to make sense of what agents produce. When researchers return to a long-horizon run, they must evaluate work they did not monitor: what the agent produced, which decisions shaped those outputs, and whether those decisions served the research goal. We frame this post-run sensemaking as a representation problem across three linked levels: goal, decision, and artifact. From this framework we developed Atlas, an agentic workspace with a trajectory tree, which renders the run as a branching structure showing what the agent chose and set aside, and artifact projections over six representations. In a within-subjects study (N=14), participants reported higher decision transparency, artifact sensemaking, and goal connection with Atlas than with a standard baseline, together with substantially lower subjective workload.

This systematic literature review investigates the evolution of automated adversary emulation and autonomous penetration testing, from attack graphs and classical planning approaches to reinforcement learning and large language model (LLM) based autonomous agents. The review examines how these approaches model attacker objectives, represent target environments, select attack actions and evaluate performance. It also assesses empirical evidence concerning the validity and limitations of the Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK frameworks for representing adversary behaviour. The review will use structured academic searches, predefined eligibility criteria, transparent study selection, quality appraisal and comparative narrative synthesis. Reporting will be guided by PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S, with methodological consideration of established software-engineering systematic review guidance. Preliminary literature searches and paper retrieval have commenced. Formal screening, quality appraisal and synthesis are planned to follow the finalisation of this protocol

Compiling quantum algorithms for real devices involves hard optimization problems that can decide whether an algorithm runs at scale. We present a general method for solving such problems with AI agents, with every result certified. It builds on autoresearch loops, in which agents iteratively improve programs against a fixed evaluator and which have recently improved quantum cryptanalysis circuits, and adds two elements: a frozen, exact verifier certifies every result, and this verifier, together with the challenge around it, is built by an agent that formulates the problem with a researcher and validates the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results before any solution exists. The method applies to any optimization problem whose solutions can be verified exactly and efficiently. We apply it to three compilation problems in quantum simulation, namely fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis. In each, the agents improved substantially on published or standard constructions, reducing the cost being optimized by up to 73% at the largest sizes tested and outperforming a state-of-the-art optimizer for fermion-to-qubit encodings. Every submission is a program accompanied by its agent's notes, so the ideas behind each improvement are recorded in human-readable form; later agents built on them, and we describe them here. These results open the way to automated, certified discovery across quantum circuit design and beyond.

This protocol describes a scoping review aimed at mapping the scientific literature on computerized systems, with or without artificial intelligence (AI), that automate quality auditing processes in healthcare services. Quality auditing supports patient safety and the identification of nonconformities; however, it is often a manual process based on data extraction from medical records and checklists organized in spreadsheets, placing a substantial workload on Quality Departments. Computerized systems, such as audit software, dashboards, rule-based systems, robotic process automation (RPA), machine learning, and natural language processing, have the potential to reduce this workload, improve information traceability and the resolution of nonconformities, and support evidence-based decision-making. However, the available evidence on this topic is scattered and heterogeneous, and no previous or ongoing reviews addressing this subject have been identified. The review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, with searches conducted in national and international databases and grey literature sources, without restrictions on language or publication year. Study selection and data extraction will be performed by two independent reviewers, and the results will be presented in tables, figures, and an evidence map, accompanied by a narrative synthesis. The analysis will seek to characterize the systems, the quality dimensions audited, the technologies employed, and the benefits, barriers, and limitations associated with their implementation. Thus, the review is expected to identify knowledge gaps and inform future research and technological development in this emerging field.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract—Contemporary enterprise Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are on the brink of systemic collapse driven by three converging factors: exponential alert fatigue (>25,000 uninvestigated alerts daily per enterprise), acute global cybersecurity workforce shortages, and the emergence of automated, machine-speed cyber threats executing multi-stage Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) in sub-minute time horizons. Traditional Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms rely on brittle, rigid, hard-coded linear playbooks that fail when adversaries deviate slightly from known MITRE ATT&CK patterns. The paradigm of the Autonomous AI-Driven SOC (Autonomous SOC) establishes a transformative architecture that replaces rigid rule engines with specialized collaborative Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) powered by fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In an Autonomous SOC, decentralized cognitive agents autonomously triage alerts, execute deep forensic graph correlation, synthesize non-linear incident playbooks, isolate compromised endpoints via zero-trust API invocations, and conduct automated counter-adversarial negotiations. However, deploying autonomous agentic execution in mission-critical defensive infrastructure exposes severe risks: catastrophic hallucination loops during remediation, prompt injection propagation across defensive pipelines, decision deadlock, and unauthorized disruption of legitimate enterprise operations. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Autonomous SOC architectures. We formalize incident response as a decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under dynamic threat uncertainty, model consensus verification over cryptographic remediation DAGs, and establish a dual-tier human-on-the-loop (HOTL) safety gating mechanism. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise SOC evaluation testbed spanning 10,000 multi-stage attack scenarios across real-world enterprise topologies. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our multi-agent autonomous framework slashes Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) from 18.4 minutes to 4.2 seconds and Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) from 42.6 minutes to 18.2 seconds (a 99.3% reduction) while preserving a 99.6% remediation accuracy against MITRE ATT&CK kill chains. Finally, we formulate open challenges in adversarial prompt-injection resilience, continuous defensive co-evolution, and liability attribution under international cyber law.

Abstract Engaging community in stakeholder processes is important to the future viability and benefit of society. Research suggests that situational awareness factors of problem‐solving and transferable skills are key processes needed for successful community engagement. This study examined undergraduate student situational awareness using problem‐solving capacity and level of transferable skills in combination with student academic performance outcomes to determine overall capacity for community engagement. The purpose of this research was to discern if there was a predictive effect between student situational awareness and the instructional outcomes of a community engagement course. A pre‐ and post‐test research design using an event‐contingent survey sampling approach was used to determine potential for community engagement. Results indicated that students that had cognitive components of situational awareness including perception, comprehension, and projection were also likely to have transferable skills including reflection (pre‐course M = 3.88 to post‐course M = 4.02) and communication skills (pre‐course M = 4.19 to post‐course M = 4.24). Results of this research provide key takeaways to enhance student learning in the context of problem‐solving within a community engagement context. Helping students develop capacities and to see themselves as engaged problem solvers can provide an important set of skills to future community engagement professionals.

This chapter explores the dual role of artificial intelligence (AI) in international higher education, highlighting its potential to integrate skill-based training with value-oriented development across various cultural contexts. By utilizing continuous surveys and interviews conducted with both local and international students and faculty members from Belarus, Uzbekistan, and China, this study explores the perceptions, adoption, and integration of AI tools within sustainability-focused curricula. The findings, presented as recommendations, aim to balance technological efficiency with a human-centered approach to education, by offering a framework for culturally sensitive AI integration which aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Furthermore, the recommendations emphasize curriculum development, faculty training, and institutional policies to ensure that AI supports the dual mission of higher education. The chapter was prepared within the research project “Develop a concept for using artificial intelligence to ensure the quality of the educational process in a higher education institution.“

This paper develops a decision support system that ranks tourism-subsidy programs for individuals according to their travel behavior. Current tourism promotion policies in Korea distribute benefits through first-come-first-served mechanisms that ignore differences in traveler preferences. We address this by constructing individual-specific, penalized behavioral features — a baseline travel-propensity term and a distance-sensitivity term — using Zero-Truncated Negative Binomial (ZT-NB) models, grouping travelers with machine-learning-based Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) clustering, and ranking policies for each traveler through an explicit eligibility filter followed by segment similarity, geographic distance, and Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)-based semantic similarity for natural language processing. Using 2024 Korea Tourism Survey data (n=3616 multi-destination travelers), we identify seven exploratory traveler segments and assess their stability by resampling the full pipeline. In a revealed-preference leave-one-out evaluation, scoring destinations by individual-specific behavioral features improves Hit@10 over random and nearest-neighbor baselines, but does not exceed a coarse region-match heuristic or a homogeneous-data artifact control, and remains below a simple pooled distance coefficient; the pooled (sample-level) distance effect and the single largest segment are the components that survive these controls. We therefore frame the artificial-intelligence contribution as exploratory behavioral segmentation and relevance ranking rather than demonstrated individual-level personalization, and the engineering application as a decision-support prototype rather than a validated mechanism for increasing travel uptake.

Disasters in urban areas are increasingly becoming complicated and this has required resilient positioning, communication and situational-awareness technologies of emergency responders. In this review, the potential of BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS)-based individual rescue equipment in responding to disasters in urban and constructed settings will be discussed. A structured literature review was conducted to study representative rescue devices, including smart helmets, intelligent life jackets and personal positioning terminals, based on their technical functions and uses in disasters. The review combines the current capabilities of BDS-based positioning, satellite short-message communication, sensing integration and emergency information support. The findings indicate that BDS-based rescue systems can be used to enhance responder localisation, emergency communication and operational coordination particularly in situations where the terrestrial communication infrastructure is damaged or unavailable. However, they are constrained by urban signal blockage, multipath and non-line-of-sight effects, indoor positioning, power consumption and system integration problems. It is possible to note that the primary benefit of BDS, when compared to other GNSS constellations, is not necessarily a more accurate positioning in all circumstances, but a set of competitive PNT services and satellite short-message communication service. It also needs to be enhanced regarding hybrid positioning, multi-sensor fusion, low-power device design and integration with smart-city and digital-twin emergency-management platforms. These advances are essential to transform BDS-enabled rescue devices from standalone tools into components of resilient urban emergency-response networks.

Long horizon agentic tasks are now pushing LLM agents past their context window. To continue the task, the agent scaffold has to free up the context window, a process known as context compaction. Compaction is generally lossy by design: agents can silently lose task constraints, instructions, or their reasoning behind earlier decisions. Although compaction is a standard component of coding agent scaffolds, it has not been studied systematically with frontier models on realistic, long horizon agentic tasks. Previous work evaluate smaller open weight models on toy or synthetic trajectories. We fix the agent scaffold (OpenCode), implement five compaction strategies inside it, and evaluate three frontier models on three long horizon benchmarks (PaperBench, ProgramBench, PostTrainBench). For the two 1M context models, the compaction threshold does not measurably affect the task performance, whereas GPT-5.3-Codex, the model with the smallest context window, performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench and, less clearly, on PostTrainBench. No compaction method outperforms default self-summarization, and methods that discard more content cost some models up to 20 points while leaving other models the same. Compaction can, however, silently remove task constraints: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task's anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat, instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do are dropped around 6 times more than specifications of what to build. We argue that current benchmarks are compaction-friendly: i.e., the objective is fixed and the agent's progress stays on disk, so most of what compaction discards can be recovered, except constraints that don't exist anywhere else.

Abstract Over several decades, machine learning systems—often described with the double metaphor “artificial intelligence”—have become indispensable computational tools in the flow and mediation of economic and social capital. These systems can, on the surface, appear to deepen the dialectic of enlightenment identified by Horkheimer and Adorno by enabling ever greater domination over natural systems and human agency. They therefore generate widespread concern that computational advances endanger the security and autonomy of human subjects, especially in the sphere of production and exchange. Contemporary social theory offers conceptual tools that go beyond received categories of domination and autonomy, however, to provide a reanalysis of machine learning systems and their implication in social dynamics and economic relations. This chapter focuses on the ways large language model (LLM) systems demonstrate complex affinities with theories of mimesis and simulacrum, and therefore how such systems and require a rethinking of performativity and artifice. Recent queer critique—in which reflection on computational systems and simulacra is proliferating—and contemporary social theory, when read together, thus reveal how rhetoric about LLMs demonstrates slippages between agency, performance, reproduction, representation, and meaning that must be unpacked historically and conceptually before metaphors of the “artificial” and “intelligence” can carry analytical weight in addressing today’s socioeconomic relations. Ultimately, this theoretical-conceptual reading highlights the stakes of the problem of truth in systems where artifice manifests both socially and computationally.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: As AI increasingly becomes a collaborator in scientific research, its impact may extend beyond improving ideas to reshaping how they are evaluated, attributed, and perceived by humans. Yet existing research has largely examined these dimensions in isolation. We present a unified empirical study of Human-AI scientific ideation, investigating two complementary perspectives: i) how AI collaboration shapes scientific ideas and their evaluation, and ii) how firsthand collaboration reshapes human perceptions of AI. Through a shared experimental setting involving Human-AI and Human-Human research teams, human and LLM evaluators, collaboration-provenance analysis, and participant surveys, we uncover several counterintuitive findings. First, AI collaboration shows no significant advantage in human-evaluated idea quality, while iterative revision consistently improves quality. Second, AI judges can approximate human scores yet disagree on idea rankings; notably, an AI judge favors AI-assisted proposals without a corresponding advantage in human evaluations. Third, collaboration provenance remains only partially detectable, revealing substantial overlap between Human-AI and Human-Human scientific outputs. Finally, firsthand AI collaboration is associated with greater perceived usefulness but smaller efficiency gains than expected, suggesting a nuanced recalibration of human expectations. Overall, our findings challenge the notion that AI's value in scientific ideation lies primarily in producing better ideas, revealing instead its broader influence on scientific creation, evaluation, attribution, and human perceptions.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Synthetic route planning is a core learning objective in university organic chemistry, yet a challenging one requiring the development of advanced problem-solving skills. Existing computational tools often propose routes beyond the intended curriculum, limiting their suitability as learning resources. In this work, we introduce Retro-Learn, an educational retrosynthesis platform that integrates a curriculum-aligned reaction template library with large language model interfaces. The platform incorporates selected aspects of pedagogical content knowledge by aligning available reactions with the scope and sequence of instruction. An agent skill and a web-based chatbot enable route generation and visualization through natural language interaction. Evaluation using cumulative chapter-specific template libraries showed how the addition of reaction knowledge enables new routes and shorter solutions. Blind assessments of undergraduate examination problems showed higher mean chemical correctness scores than those of database-derived routes and scores comparable to or higher than those of general-purpose language models. Student survey responses indicated a plurality preference for Retro-Learn over general-purpose tools as a synthesis-planning learning aid. These findings illustrate how curriculum-specific chemical informatics and language model interfaces can translate pedagogical considerations into computational support for organic chemistry learning.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Accurate ambulance travel time estimation is critical for emergency medical dispatch, yet existing decision-support practices often rely on static lookup tables or simplified assumptions regarding how ambulance travel time differs from ordinary passenger-car travel. For instance, they assume ambulances simply travel a fixed percentage (e.g., 5%) faster than ordinary passenger cars. However, such assumptions are rarely validated using real ambulance operational data and may fail to capture the effects of trip priority, temporal context, and origin-destination. We address these limitations using historical ambulance trips from the Skåne region in Sweden. Our analysis reveals that ambulance travel times vary substantially by hour, day, and trip priority, and that commercial navigation systems fail to capture emergency-specific dynamics. We contribute a machine learning system to more accurately estimate ambulance travel time. To make the system interpretable, we explored SHapley Additive exPlanations and permutation importance techniques to ensure that our system captures operationally meaningful patterns.

English language education in Saudi Arabia is undergoing transforming amid broader economic, educational, and technological reforms. English plays an important role in higher education, professional development, internationalization, and participation in the knowledge-based economy, while young Saudis increasingly engage with English through social media, entertainment, gaming, and digital communication. Generative AI is also reshaping how learners access, produce, practice, and evaluate language. However, Saudi EFL research often treats language policy, classroom practice, learner attitudes, and technology as separate domains, potentially obscuring their dynamic interactions. Drawing on language policy and planning, language ecology, human-capital perspectives, and sociocultural approaches, this conceptual article proposes the Saudi EFL Ecological Transformation Framework (SEETF). The framework conceptualizes Saudi EFL as a dynamic ecology shaped by three interacting forces: language policy, economic transformation, and youth language practices, with generative AI functioning as a cross-cutting mediating force that alters the speed, visibility, and form of these interactions. It emphasizes policy enactment, learner agency, informal language practices, and asymmetries in influence and in the pace of change across institutional and societal contexts. The article advances seven conceptual propositions and argues that the future of Saudi EFL depends not on expanding English instruction but on coordinating these forces across differing timescales and degrees of institutional control.

Understanding how disaster education enhances awareness and preparedness is crucial for improving community resilience to disasters. Although Japan widely implements routine evacuation drills, these may not foster an autonomous understanding of hazard characteristics. Conversely, specialized disaster education—such as survivor talks or field activities—provides deeper engagement; however, empirical evidence of its association with later awareness and preparedness remains limited. This study examined whether specialized disaster education correlates with higher disaster awareness and preparedness among young adults in Japan compared to standard evacuation drills. A nationwide online questionnaire survey obtained valid responses from 1,479 participants in their twenties. Respondents were divided into Specialized Education and Standard Drill groups, and their awareness and preparedness behaviors were analyzed using descriptive statistics and ordinal logistic regression with partial proportional-odds models. The results showed that the Specialized Education group had significantly higher awareness of local disaster risks and greater preparedness than those in the Standard Drill group, who were often neutral or undecided. Among the key indicators, the positive impact of specialized disaster education surpassed that of demographic characteristics and past disaster experience. Notably, regression analysis revealed that education was particularly effective in raising awareness from low to moderate levels, highlighting its role in raising hazard awareness. These findings underscore the value of additional specialized disaster education in supplementing standard drills.

Sales pipelines measure commercial possibilities, but they do not always reveal whether customers are ready to make decisions. This conceptual article examines the difference between buyer interest and verified commitment in business development serving the American market. Drawing on published research on B2B buying, digital channels, artificial intelligence and employee engagement, it introduces the Commitment Gap as a practitioner lens and proposes the CARE framework: Customer Reality, Alignment, Relationship Credibility and Execution Ownership. The paper uses a narrative review and an illustrative implementation framework rather than original field data. It argues that revenue forecasts become more credible when sellers verify buying actions, respect customer autonomy and coordinate promises across teams. The proposed framework remains unvalidated and is offered for future empirical testing.

Meat and fish vendors in wet public markets are frequently exposed to wet work, raw animal products, and prolonged working hours, increasing their risk of occupational skin conditions. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of skin conditions among meat and fish vendors in the Old and New San Fernando Public Markets and examine the relationships among their perception of preventive measures, hygienic practices, and prevalence of skin conditions. A quantitative, descriptive-correlational cross-sectional design was employed among 152 vendors selected through purposive sampling. The study was completed in May 2026. Data were collected using a researcher-made questionnaire adapted from the Occupational Skin Diseases Exposure Scales (OSDES-16) and analyzed using frequency, percentage, prevalence, weighted mean, standard deviation, and Pearson product-moment correlation at a 0.05 level of significance. Results showed that lichenification or skin thickening had the highest self-reported prevalence (63.8%), followed by dryness and itching (63.2%). Respondents demonstrated a high level of perception of preventive measures (M = 3.11, SD = 0.68) and hygienic practices (M = 2.84, SD = 0.63). Significant positive relationships were found between skin-condition prevalence and preventive measures (r = .252, p = .002), skin-condition prevalence and hygienic practices (r = .345, p < .001), and hygienic practices and preventive measures (r = .550, p < .001). Skin conditions remain common despite high perception, highlighting the need for strengthened occupational health interventions and improved workplace conditions.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Cross-domain sequential recommendation aims to alleviate data sparsity and cold-start problems by transferring useful preference knowledge across domains. However, users exhibit varying degrees of preference consistency across domains, while existing methods often rely on global alignment objectives or coarse-grained transfer strategies. Such approaches may introduce irrelevant information and provide limited flexibility in adapting semantic representations to individual user preferences. To address these challenges, we propose BGAFlow, a personalized framework that combines state-adaptive semantic evolution with user-specific transfer control. BGAFlow first establishes a shared semantic space through unified dual-domain pretraining with user profiles inferred by a large language model (LLM). Based on latent interest overlap, it then estimates a personalized horizon to determine the appropriate transfer extent for each user. To enable semantic adaptation, BGAFlow constructs a conditional Bezier curve as a geometric reference and learns a residual flow that progressively refines the trajectory based on intermediate preference states. The learned flow incorporates dynamic preference feedback to adjust transfer directions, while recommendation supervision and trajectory regularization encourage effective and smooth adaptation. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that BGAFlow consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating the benefits of personalized transfer control and state-adaptive semantic evolution.

The work weaves Islamic theology, analytical frameworks, and the story of reality into a single narrative arc, opening and closing with Bismillah ir-Rahman ir-Rahim. College students' level of psychological resilience exerts a direct influence on their mental health and academic development, and constitutes a key pathway to more effectively fulfilling the fundamental mission of fostering virtue through education and enhancing the quality of higher education. Leveraging the advantages of digital intelligence technologies to empower blended teaching reform in the cultivation of college students' psychological resilience not only responds to the developmental imperatives of the intelligentization of higher education, but also serves the practical need to enhance students' psychological resilience and the educational effectiveness of fostering virtue through education. This paper explores a pathway for empowering blended teaching reform in the cultivation of college students' psychological resilience through the following approaches: upholding technological iteration to advance a resilience-oriented educational philosophy, thereby innovating teaching concepts; optimizing the allocation of digital intelligence resources to support precise learner profiling; creating situated experiential learning platforms to activate resilience-protective mechanisms; constructing a sound intelligent educational ecosystem to foster a supportive environment; and establishing a robust human–AI collaborative mechanism to improve developmental assessment. The study aims to promote the transformation of mental health education from a knowledge-centered to a competency-centered paradigm, thereby laying a foundation for cultivating a new generation of talent equipped with both sound psychological qualities and digital intelligence literacy.

Question paper leakage has emerged as a critical national crisis, compromising the fairness and integrity of academic and competitive assessments across India. Incidents affecting NEET-UG, UGC-NET, CSIR-NET, and multiple state Public Service Commission examinations have impacted over one crore students annually, eroding public trust in the examination system. The fundamental vulnerability lies in centralized human-dependent workflows spanning question paper setting, printing, physical transportation, storage, and distribution. Current security measures rely entirely on physical safeguards such as sealed envelopes, armed guards, and secure strongrooms, which fail catastrophically when any single individual in the chain is compromised. This paper proposes a comprehensive blockchain-based question paper leakage prevention system that integrates Blockchain technology, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), and Machine Learning (ML) into a unified secure examination framework. The system replaces centralized trust with distributed cryptographic proof, ensuring that no single person can leak examination materials without leaving an immutable, traceable record. GenAI enables dynamic question paper generation, eliminating preexisting papers that can be leaked weeks in advance. Machine Learning powers real-time social media monitoring for leak detection and forensic tracing of leaked content back to its source. Digital watermarking embeds unique forensic identifiers into each printed copy, enabling precise source identification. Smart contracts enforce time-locked distribution windows, ensuring that question papers do not exist in decryptable form until exactly thirty minutes before the examination.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: The seventeenth essay in Brainstorming with the Enemy was written on the morning of 22 October 2026. It began with transport, trains, trucks, drones and cars, and the artificial intelligence that already plans their movements one fleet at a time, and turned when the machine was asked to stop thinking like a transport consultant and start thinking like a zoologist. Schooling fish, flocking starlings, pelicans, lobsters, penguins, ants and bees show that nature never optimises the vehicle; it optimises the collective. The salp, a chain of animals in which each member swims by its own jet and none pulls the others, is taken as the model: coordination that widens each member's options while creating value for all, a cooperation biologists call by-product mutualism. The essay separates two goods that moving machines can share. Time, the speed a convoy gains when braking signals travel faster than any human reaction, belongs to every member and needs no payment; energy, the drag saved behind a leader, is unequal and needs settling. It then turns the salp into a warning: salps are clones, and a chain of machines running the same software fails as one, as the processionary caterpillars that circle a vase until they starve already show. It proposes the Salp Standard, five clauses for coupling moving machines, from smart trailers and parcels to drones and self-driving cars, without a head, without a single lineage and with the right of any member to stop the chain; makes three requests, to vehicle and coupler makers, to China's fleet operators and to the Swiss cantons; and gives, as an addendum, the Coupling Clearing, a rule for sharing the energy gain, with three predictions and what would refute each. Concepts proposed by the author: the Salp Standard; the Coupling Clearing; the Bestiary Axis. Written in part with Claude (Anthropic), an AI model. The ideas, editorial decisions and responsibility for the content are the author's.

Frontier coding agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Yet, they still face challenges when building objects meant to be assembled in the physical world, often creating invalid assemblies with floating, colliding, or disconnected parts. We argue that providing agents with tools for assembling builds and verifying their physical feasibility is sufficient for them to produce physically valid assemblies that still adhere to input prompts. Focusing on the domain of LEGO brick builds, we present BrickWright, a framework for generating physically feasible brick builds from text or image prompts using pre-trained agents, where a build is physically feasible if it uses only real parts, has no colliding or floating parts, and forms a connected structure if possible. BrickWright guides agents to create builds by writing code with BrickLayer, a Python toolkit with two main components: an ergonomic brick assembly API that halves inference cost compared to working in raw LDraw, and a validator that provides feedback on physical feasibility. Whereas baseline agents achieve physical validity rates ranging from only 9% (GPT-6 Luna) to 69% (GPT-6 Astra), BrickWright-guided agents achieve 100% validity on a sample of 512 prompts, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight agents and maintaining it for stronger agents. Additionally, they outperform specialized models on the text-to-brick task. Code is available on our project page: https://avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright/
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Abstract This paper examines translocal bridge building in the context of extractivism. The authors understand translocal bridge building as the forging of coalitions across geographies and differences. The authors examine efforts to establish such connections between organizations and extraction sites in the Netherlands and Guatemala along seven analytical dimensions. The authors’ aim is to understand the dynamics and intricacies of such experiences and draw lessons for translocal coalition building. The authors’ analysis suggests that bridge building is not always the most suitable strategy for organizations working at extraction sites. Place-based realities require continuous organizational adaptation to specific territorial needs in order to avoid new dynamics of exclusion. At the same time, the authors suggest that deliberate bridge building—facilitated by continuous commitment, personal connections, and intrinsic motivations rather than institutionalized collaboration—offers an opportunity to zoom out and address shared injustices amid the global patterns of extractivism. Such connections are strengthened when there is mutual recognition of place-specific realities and differences. This paper offers grounded and applicable lessons for translocal coalition building in the context of extractivism and social and environmental contestation more broadly.
topics: Global trade, sustainability, and social impact
