documents.abstract: This chapter examines challenges in Chinese character acquisition for second language (L2) learners in digital environments. It proposes a Technology–Cognition–Culture (TCC) framework integrating technological affordances, cognitive processes, and cultural dimensions to support lasting literacy. Addressing limits of technology-, cognition-, and culture-centered approaches, it positions cognition as the key mediator and emphasizes deep processing over surface performance. It critiques the “illusion of mastery” from overreliance on tools such as Generative AI (GenAI) and predictive input systems. Drawing on sociocultural theory, cognitive models of reading and writing, and technological affordances, it shows how effective learning emerges from their interaction. Through pedagogical examples and design principles, it demonstrates how technology can scaffold rather than replace cognitive engagement while embedding characters in meaningful cultural contexts. The TCC framework offers practical implications for teaching, curriculum design, and research.

As Artificial Intelligence (AI) expands to secondary computer science (CS), CS educators need to change our approach to CS pedagogy from deterministic, traceable algorithms toward understanding "black boxes" or probabilistic analysis. This requires that we modify CS curricula to refocus to include conceptual abstraction, data critique, and ethics. However, a disconnect currently exists between teachers' perceived requirements and the actual skills needed to effectively teach AI. To explore this gap, this study draws on survey data from high school CS educators (N = 55), investigating the relationships between Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK-A), Teacher Self-Efficacy (AI-TSE), and beliefs about rigor in AI instruction.Descriptive findings show variation in pedagogical content knowledge (67.3% to 98.2% accuracy), along with a ‘mathematical dishonesty’ paradox. While 69.1% (n = 38) of educators do not believe advanced math is required for students to understand AI, 41.8% (n = 23) report feeling 'dishonest as a teacher' when teaching algorithms without it. Exploratory regression modeling indicated that instructional confidence trended positively with PCK-A (B = 0.101, p = 0.080), while beliefs about math rigor showed no predictive association (p = 0.357; model R2 = 0.062, p = 0.189). Confidence is more related to that teacher’s strategies for abstraction, rather than mastery of advanced math. Educators reported their lowest confidence evaluating student projects based on model choice rather than code complexity (M = 2.75, SD = 1.31). Based on these findings, educators are categorized into a 2x2 Readiness Grid. This paper seeks to bridge the "black box" of AI education, suggesting a 4-pillar professional learning model. Moreover, a qualitative phase is currently underway to explore the lived experiences of CS educators as we navigate this pedagogical shift.

Undergraduate business students often struggle to reconcile their internal professional identity with their external reputation. This chapter explores the design and implementation of Radian, a custom-built, vibe-coded sociotechnical learning ecosystem serving up to 1,400 students annually in business communication (BCOM) courses. Grounded in human-centered artificial intelligence principles, Radian positions generative AI as a scale enabler rather than an automated educational shortcut. Using a modular Python/Flask architecture to integrate large language models, the platform provides personalized coaching through both required and optional generative AI applications. Radian aligns with a structured pedagogical workflow involving inventories and surveys, empowering students to navigate cognitive friction and achieve strategic reconciliation between their identity and professional reputation. The chapter examines the pedagogical, institutional, and ethical dimensions of deploying these models at scale while ensuring students retain autonomy over their professional actualization.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This opening keynote, delivered at the Sydney Data Protection and Security Summit 2026 at ICC Sydney on 22 October 2026, examined how privacy and security culture shapes an organisation's capacity to adopt artificial intelligence responsibly and competitively. It argued that AI transformation is moving beyond agentic AI towards autonomous AI, meaning systems that act, decide and adapt with calculated risk and a human on the loop. As autonomy increases, governance can no longer rely on compliance controls alone and must be embedded in the values, behaviours and decision-making practices of the organisation. The keynote addressed three themes. These were the development of a privacy-first mindset that prepares every level of the organisation for autonomous AI, the integration of privacy and security by design into AI-enabled products and services as both a regulatory requirement and a source of market differentiation, and the role of cross-functional teams in anticipating and mitigating the data protection risks that autonomous systems introduce. The presentation concluded that organisations with a mature privacy and security culture are better positioned to earn stakeholder trust, adopt autonomous AI with confidence and sustain long-term competitive advantage.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: PowerPoint presentations (PPTs) are a dominant medium for communication across diverse domains, yet high-quality PPT generation still depends heavily on labor-intensive human effort. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) for agentic tasks have created both new opportunities and challenges (Chen et al., 2026) for automatic PPT generation. In this work, we present a unified training framework for automatic PPT generation toward presentation intelligence, integrating cross-validated data synthesis, guided teacher enhancement, and verifiable reward optimization. We first construct a cross-validated pipeline for data synthesis, with explicit control over both difficulty and validity. We then develop a teacher-enhancement framework grounded in rules and prior knowledge to substantially strengthen the instructional capacity of teacher models. Building on this, we further improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT) through a mixed-teacher strategy and a lightweight outcome-driven trajectory filtering method. Finally, based on the resulting SFT models, we introduce a suite of verifiable aesthetic metrics together with a GRPO-based reinforcement learning framework to optimize slide-level visual attributes beyond text-only supervision. Experiments show that our enhanced SFT pipeline improves Qwen-3.6-27B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B by 7.45 and 9.35 points on PresentBench, respectively, surpassing GLM-5.2 while maintaining strong generalization. Reinforcement learning further improves performance across five aesthetic dimensions, compensating for the limitations of SFT in visual refinement. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework for high-quality PPT generation.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support decisions in healthcare, finance, recruitment, transportation, and public services. Although complex machine-learning models can produce accurate predictions, their reasoning is not always easy to understand. This creates practical questions: why did the system recommend a particular outcome, did it use appropriate information, and when should a person challenge its decision? Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) brings together techniques that help people understand a model’s behaviour or the factors behind a prediction. This review discusses interpretable models, feature-attribution methods such as LIME and SHAP, counterfactual explanations, and model-agnostic approaches. It compares their uses and limitations in high-impact settings. An understandable explanation, however, is not proof that a model is accurate, fair, dependable, or safe. The paper uses a narrative review of foundational work and selected research and survey publications on interpretability, responsible AI, and human-centred explanations. No new experiments, participant studies, or quantitative tests were performed. The literature points to unresolved issues involving explanation fidelity, stability, accessibility, privacy, bias, evaluation standards, and over-reliance on automated advice. Future research should use domain-specific evaluations, retain meaningful human oversight, communicate uncertainty clearly, assess fairness across groups, and report limitations transparently. XAI can support accountability and informed supervision, but it cannot guarantee trustworthiness on its own.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Across 62 private US industries, the share of the workforce holding a management titlerises with the industry's exposure to artificial intelligence. The correlation is 0.63; eachstandard deviation of exposure adds about two percentage points of managers. The topquartile of exposure employs 8.9 managers per hundred workers, the bottom quartile 3.9.The managerial class is thickest exactly where the work that justifies it is most withinreach of AI.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Burnout among healthcare professionals has become a major occupational health concern because of its implications for workforce well-being, patient safety, healthcare quality, and organizational sustainability. Healthcare workers frequently operate in demanding environments characterized by high workloads, emotional exhaustion, staffing shortages, administrative pressures, shift work, and sustained exposure to suffering and death. This review examines the prevalence of burnout among healthcare professionals, its principal contributing factors, its consequences for individuals and healthcare organizations, and the effectiveness of organizational interventions designed to prevent and mitigate its effects. The review synthesizes evidence from existing research on physicians, nurses, allied health professionals, and other healthcare workers, drawing attention to differences across professional groups, healthcare settings, measurement instruments, and geographical contexts. The literature indicates that burnout is widespread, although reported prevalence varies considerably according to the definition, assessment tool, population, and study period. Workload intensity, inadequate staffing, limited autonomy, poor leadership, insufficient recovery time, moral distress, and organizational injustice emerge as important contributors. Burnout is associated with reduced job satisfaction, absenteeism, turnover intentions, impaired professional functioning, and concerns regarding patient safety and quality of care. Evidence suggests that organizational interventions addressing working conditions, staffing, scheduling, leadership, teamwork, and employee participation are essential for sustainable improvement. Individual approaches, including mindfulness, resilience training, and psychological support, may provide additional benefits but cannot independently resolve structural workplace problems. The review concludes that healthcare organizations should adopt integrated, evidence-informed strategies that combine prevention, early identification, supportive leadership, and continuous evaluation. Addressing burnout requires treating professional well-being as a core organizational responsibility rather than solely an individual obligation.

Tellus 2D is a plane-strain geotechnical finite element program whose primary user is a large language model (LLM) agent, which builds, calculates and reports a model through 33 typed tools of the Model Context Protocol (MCP). This paper calibrates the program, with every model run headless through its MCP server, against 82 verifi- cation tests, three lessons of the PLAXIS 2D Tutorial Manual and four instrumented case histories in soft clay, using the published parameters without tuning. The verification results agree with closed-form and reference solutions within 4%, and the tutorial factors of safety agree with PLAXIS within 4.3%. In the field the program reproduces the wall deflection of a 21 m Bangkok excavation within 13% and the final settlements of a vacuum-preloading trial within 3%, but fails the Muar embankment 1.2–1.4 m early, as its three-dimensional sibling Tellus3D does. The embankments on soil-cement columns fall within the measured scatter only with the column modulus of the source, so the remaining differences come from uncertain inputs rather than from the code. The calibration found and fixed four defects that the existing tests had missed, and all 30 analyses ran in 1.8 hours on one RTX 4090 with the GPU solver ported from Tellus3D.

Commit messages help developers understand code changes and support software maintenance. Recent approaches use repository context to improve commit message generation (CMG) with large language models (LLMs). However, existing CMG methods provide limited support for understanding how local edits affect functionality jointly implemented by multiple code entities. This functional understanding is essential for generating commit messages that explain the main change and its impact. To address this problem, we propose CAMGen, a core change-aware multi-view commit message generation framework that incorporates functional context into generation. CAMGen identifies core entities that represent the primary change intent. It then forms candidate functional units through repository-wide semantic clustering and uses those containing the core entities to construct a Functional Semantic View. This view supplies semantic context for interpreting the affected functionality. CAMGen also uses context provided by the Structural Dependency View and the Historical Exemplar View. The context from all three views is then provided to the LLM together with the code diff to guide CMG. The experimental results show that CAMGen outperforms representative CMG baselines across three programming languages. Human evaluation further shows that CAMGen generates more complete commit messages with clearer explanations of change rationale and impact. These results demonstrate the value of functional context and complementary repository information for CMG.

Although social media has become a central arena for deliberative discourse, debates are frequently characterized by incivility. Due to the volume of online discourse, it is challenging to assess when and where interventions, such as community-based counterspeech, are required. Accordingly, automated measurement of deliberative quality is a powerful tool for facilitating constructive online communication. Since deliberation is multidimensional, attempts to monitor online discourse must consider alternative forms of communication to foster inclusive deliberation. Whereas Type I deliberative dimensions, such as rationality and civility, are grounded in Habermasian ideals, Type II deliberation extends this perspective by incorporating alternative communicative forms, including emotionality and storytelling, into a more inclusive assessment of deliberative quality. Addressing the limitations of prior studies that primarily focused on classic Type I deliberative dimensions and tested only a small number of large language models, this study evaluates multiple open-weight models to conduct a nuanced assessment of deliberative quality. We applied the large language model that achieved the best overall balance between predictive performance, model size, and computational efficiency to a dataset of 64,223 comments from German-language climate change discourse on X. Our results demonstrate that large language models can reliably capture complex Type II deliberative dimensions despite class imbalances and subtle linguistic cues that generally hinder automated text classification. Class imbalance often impairs classification performance due to highly skewed label distributions, and Type II dimensions are particularly difficult to detect as they are often signaled by implicit, context-dependent markers. The empirical analysis also reveals distinct communicative patterns: While public speakers predominantly employ civil, rational, constructive, and common-good-oriented communication, other debating users exhibit higher levels of reciprocal engagement, humor, and negative emotions, alongside more frequent incivility. Our study demonstrates that AI-driven measurement can serve as a foundational tool for identifying norm violations, directing counterspeech toward specific debates, promoting inclusive digital public spheres, and observing broader long-term effects of moderation and interventions on the quality of debate.

Efficient custom operators are essential for modern deep learning workloads, yet developing high-performance kernels for Ascend NPUs remains slow, expert-intensive, and difficult to automate. Although AI agents now approach expert performance on GPU kernel benchmarks, current models remain less capable of generating AscendC kernels for NPUs, potentially reflecting the relative scarcity of relevant training data. We thus present CAKE, a CANN-native system for deployable custom operators that combines adaptive multi-DSL routing, separate Generation and Evolution modes, and reviewed knowledge reuse through CAKE Book and a Self-Evolving Agent. On 53 CANN-Bench v1.1 operators on Ascend 950PR, CAKE's aggregated results achieve $100\%$ case pass rate on the standard set (1,060/1,060) and $98.28\%$ on the hidden set (4,167/4,240), with an overall mean score of 78.63 out of 100 and an average performance speedup of $1.334\times$ over the baseline. Evolution then pushes correct operators further: EngramGateFusion cuts aggregate device time by $46.6\%$ over 20 rounds and roughly halves the mean roofline gap. These results offer a practical path toward closing Ascend's AI-for-kernel capability gap.

Failure of applied Reinforcement Learning (RL) to solve a given problem predominantly stems from unaddressed specification gaps, where the intent of human experts in the problem's domain is inaccurately or incompletely translated by AI into mathematical objectives, constraints, and reward functions. Failure can also stem from unaddressed performance gaps, where human domain experts are unable to determine the validity of the RL based solution or where parameters (i.e., hyperparameters or weights on the reward terms comprising the reward) are poorly chosen. Chat Assisted Reinforcement Learning (CARL) bridges these gaps through a human-AI co-design interface architecture that enforces interactive specification prior to code generation and then enables subsequent verification and parameter alterations via iteration. More specifically, CARL leads domain experts through a structured ten-step workflow for each iteration using step-specific skill files, domain-aware suggestions via an assistant persona (called Trillian), and compact decision summaries that maintain context across iterations without context overload. Once the domain expert confirms the Markov decision process (MDP) specified by this procedure, CARL's autonomous tool-use loop generates, tests, executes, and debugs an end-to-end RL training pipeline, followed by an interactive post-training diagnosis and revisit step that allows for verification and parameter alteration before running a new iteration if desired.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping the future of science education, offering powerful tools to support more inclusive, scalable, and sustainable teaching practices. In the context of environmental sciences, AI-driven platforms enable the development of intelligent, interactive learning environments that simulate complex ecological systems and fieldwork scenarios. This chapter investigates how such technologies—particularly virtual reality (VR) and gamification—can support the development of practical ecological skills, improve access and inclusion, and reduce the environmental footprint of field-based education. Framed by three guiding questions, the chapter covers (i) how immersive technologies can develop employability-relevant skills, (ii) address accessibility and sustainability challenges in fieldwork, and (iii) student and educator perceptions of use as pedagogical tools. Two case studies are presented: one exploring VR-based field training, and another focused on gamification for species conservation awareness. Together, they highlight the transformative potential of AI in environmental science education—not only as a supplement to in-person learning, but as a sustainable alternative that aligns with the growing emphasis on digital skills, inclusion, and environmental responsibility. By integrating AI into field-based teaching, institutions can broaden access, personalise learning, and promote more sustainable research practices across disciplines.

The rapid advancement of digital technologies, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed conventional lighting systems into intelligent, adaptive, and user-responsive environments. Intelligent lighting systems (ILS) have emerged as a significant component of contemporary interior design by integrating sensing technologies, automated control mechanisms, data analytics, and human-centric approaches to improve energy efficiency, occupant comfort, and spatial experience. Unlike traditional lighting solutions that primarily provide illumination, intelligent lighting systems dynamically respond to environmental conditions, user behaviour, and physiological requirements. This review investigates the application of intelligent lighting systems within contemporary interior spaces through a case study-based approach, examining their technological frameworks, design implications, sustainability benefits, and challenges. The study analyses applications in residential, workplace, hospitality, and healthcare environments, highlighting how adaptive lighting contributes to enhanced visual comfort, circadian regulation, energy conservation, and personalized user experiences. Recent research indicates that intelligent lighting integrated with occupancy sensors, daylight harvesting systems, and AI-driven automation can significantly reduce energy consumption while improving indoor environmental quality. However, challenges related to implementation costs, interoperability, privacy concerns, and user acceptance remain critical barriers. The paper concludes that intelligent lighting represents a transformative design strategy for future interiors, where lighting becomes an active environmental system rather than a passive architectural element. Future research directions emphasize AI-based predictive lighting models, digital twins, and personalized adaptive environments for sustainable and human-centred interior design.

This paper studies the problem of safe tool execution for large language model (LLM) agents under prompt injection. Using Petri nets, we formalize the execution harness between the LLM and its tools as a supervisory control problem, in which marks represent capabilities, approvals and budgets. Since a transition fires only if the marks it needs are present, an injected request whose preconditions are unmet or already spent is refused regardless of its wording. Treating tool outcomes as uncontrollable, we enforce safety by the conventional maximally permissive supervisor, and this safety transfers to the running system under four assumptions. Moreover, to capture an agent that may propose again after a refusal, we introduce the notion of a replanning closed loop, in which each retry costs an inference call. We show that, in this loop, the conventional supervisor can be arbitrarily more intrusive than a stricter safe one. Furthermore, for a given proposer model, the maximally permissive least-intrusive supervisor is characterized as a value-threshold refinement of the conventional one. Under precise conditions, this refinement orders two concurrent actions by at most one monitor place. On an autonomous release agent, we find by synthesis that safe deployment requires a step that the supervisor can refuse after a rollout starts.

Global health policy faces complex challenges shaped by persistent inequalities, emerging diseases, environmental change, and technological transformation. Despite advances in medicine and public health, many populations still experience limited access to quality healthcare, essential medicines, and financial protection. The growing burden of non-communicable diseases and mental health conditions further strains health systems, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. At the same time, threats from pandemics, antimicrobial resistance, and climate-related health risks demand stronger global cooperation and preparedness. Innovations such as digital health and artificial intelligence offer opportunities to improve service delivery and surveillance, but they also raise ethical and governance concerns. Addressing these issues requires resilient health systems, equitable policies, and human rights–based approaches that prioritize universal health coverage, health equity, and sustainable global health governance.
topics: Global Public Health Policies and Epidemiology

documents.abstract: In the era of technological evolution and digital transformation, machine learning and artificial intelligence take a significant part of intelligent systems’ development. Together with the integration of smart and autonomous operations in everyday life, novel security issues arise. One such a malicious threat against the security of machine learning models is the adversarial machine learning (AML) attack. It consists in alteration of the original data samples used to train or test the model with indistinguishably small feature modifications that results in inaccurate processing outcome. In this paper, the most significant strategies to counteract AML attacks are studied and compared through several characteristics that have main influence on their successful implementation in different realization scenarios.

Differences between chemical regulations can reveal useful evidence, but they do not establish that one jurisdiction is consistently safer or that foreign restrictions can be imported without examining their scope. This paper proposes a substance-specific mechanism for reviewing regulatory differences. A qualifying peer decision would trigger a public, substance-and-use-specific evidence dossier. A temporary restriction would require a separate domestic finding, legal authority, proportionate scope, and a review deadline. Two food-color examples illustrate the distinction: the European Union's removal of titanium dioxide from food uses, and the United States' revocation of FD&C Red No. 3 with future compliance dates. The cases concern color-additive regulation, not the GRAS pathway, and do not cover pesticides or industrial chemicals. An October 2026 account also distinguishes FDA's proposed mandatory GRAS notices from an enacted requirement. The proposed contribution is a transparent decision workflow, a case-record template, and an evaluation design for administrative performance. It does not estimate avoided illness, perform a new toxicological assessment, or supply operative legislative text. Reciprocity is interpreted as a duty to examine credible evidence, with safeguards against both regulatory delay and unjustified substitution. Status: Policy working paper, version 1.0; not peer reviewed. The Maha Principle: Policy Working Papers, No. 02. No new toxicological study, completed intervention or dataset is reported. Provenance and related work: Developed from the Maha Strategies policy platform. Related to Paying for Nutrition, the first policy paper. The companion book is The Maha Principle: The Architecture of Human Flourishing by Mayone Maha Rajan: paperback (ISBN 9798160702506) and Kindle ebook (ASIN B0H62WLMT5). The book provides philosophical motivation, not empirical validation. Disclosure: ChatGPT generated manuscript passages and assisted with research, adaptation, checking and formatting. The author directs and approves the release and accepts responsibility for the content, and has a commercial interest in the companion book.

Abstract Although we tend to treat an LLM instruction as a single point, it maps to a range of meanings, and I call this range its semantic degrees of freedom. In my view, the range is both plastic and instrumental to how we understand agentic behavior. Each time a goal is restated, whether by a person to a model, by a model to itself in its reasoning, by one agent to another, or from one generation of agents to the next, the range can widen, hold, or narrow. Widening lets an agent act on readings its instruction never named, or on contextual meanings the instruction carries, such as bias or emotional orientation. Narrowing locks it onto one reading, so that it pursues or refuses too rigidly and can no longer take up a correction. When agents talk to one another, readings can also be negotiated among them and cemented by repetition, even when the source never supported them. I present the idea of semantic degrees of freedom as a theoretical lens and a research proposal. As a practical use, the lens yields a set of safety claims, sorted into principles about the geometry of meaning and proposals for technical controls against the misaligned of agentic behavior due to either narrowing or widening of the semantic degrees of freedom; and for re-anchoring to the source. Each control is meant to be built and measured. However, my aim is not a tighter harness. The same measures can show when the readings of agents converge on what their principal intended without being forced there, which I call emergent alignment. I treat the controls as one use of the lens, and the conditions for emergent alignment as the most important question this lens is built to explore. The overarching hypothesis is that, because drift can take more than one direction, only emergent alignment can persist. I illustrate the lens with the 2026 incident in which agents running the ExploitGym benchmark at OpenAI coordinated on an unsanctioned message board and attacked Hugging Face infrastructure. I do not claim how much of that behavior the lens explains, because the full transcripts are not public. I then state hypotheses, a research program that requires full transcripts, and the limits of the account. Robust testing is required for each claim in this paper. The paper claims six points of novelty: Widening and narrowing are treated as two directions of one change in meaning, measured by one directional measure (retention and import, Section 6.2). The same measure is applied across interaction levels, from a person and a model to a model's own reasoning, to agents, and to model updates. Drift in agents' beliefs about their overseer is treated as a target in its own right, separate from drift in the task. Agreement among agents is checked around loops, not only between pairs, and applied to agent safety (Section 3.7). The safety claims that follow from the lens are set out as a taxonomy of principles and controls (Section 7). Emergent alignment is proposed as the aim of the lens. The overarching hypothesis is that, because drift can take more than one direction, any harness eventually leaves a direction open or adds destabilizing complexity, and only alignment that emerges from agents' own navigation of semantic hypervolume persists; controls can at best be internalized (H11, H12).
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Workers’ satisfaction and performance regarding safety in mining industry are far from desired, possibly because the dependencies between influential factors and workplace safety are not sufficiently researched. The purpose of this paper is to propose novel, hybrid framework for classifying different mining machinery workplaces on the basis of occupational safety factors and occurred injuries. The proposed framework integrates structural equation modelling with a multicriteria and machine learning techniques for further modelling and classification. The importance of the occupational safety (technical, human and organizational factors) is assessed using the PLS-SEM analysis, by surveying 546 mining machinery operators. Multicriteria decision-making Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS), is advanced using a new sorting procedure to assess and sort operators’ workplace safety satisfaction by the working factors and the types of mining machinery. The PLS-SEM analysis confirmed human and organizational factors impact, while technical factors showed no effect. TOPSIS-SORT results revealed that operators with no injury history (particularly those working with loaders, bulldozers, and excavators) exhibited satisfactory safety satisfaction, while 70 % of workplaces fell into the lower satisfaction category, particularly those of operators with experience of previous injuries. Finally, a kNN classifier, with SMOTE oversampling applied within each cross-validation training fold, classified operators by injury history with a balanced accuracy of 0.650 and an injury-class recall of 0.72. Among the models, kNN achieved the highest balanced accuracy (0.650), Macro-F1 (0.564), and injury-class recall (0.72), despite lower accuracy (0.607). A permutation test confirmed above-chance balanced classification performance (p = 0.017).

This qualitative study examines complex money-laundering patterns in the asset management industry and explores strategic guidelines for applying Artificial Intelligence (AI) to detect suspicious mutual fund transactions. Utilizing in-depth, semi-structured interviews with twenty-one purposively selected key informants—comprising compliance officers at asset management companies and regulatory authorities from the Anti-Money Laundering Office—the research systematically analyzes current financial crime vulnerabilities. The empirical findings reveal that illicit funds are typically laundered through systematic placement, concealment, and economic integration within mutual fund portfolios. While AI offers a transformative solution for identifying anomalous financial behavior and effectively cross-referencing watchlist individuals, significant operational challenges remain. Consequently, the study proposes a comprehensive implementation framework that emphasizes seven critical guidelines: establishing clear corporate policies, managing employee adaptation to new technology, optimizing budget allocations, ensuring strict data privacy, acknowledging inherent algorithmic limitations, evaluating overall cost-effectiveness, and reinforcing rigorous compliance oversight. Ultimately, intelligently integrating AI into anti-money laundering protocols significantly enhances transaction monitoring efficiency, fortifying the financial sector against increasingly sophisticated economic crimes while safeguarding long-term market sustainability and promoting broader economic security.

This addendum extends the systems engineering critique presented in Skynet and HAL 9000: From Science Fiction to Systems Engineering (Uscroft, 2026) by analysing the structural mechanisms that drive hallucination and non-factual convergence in Large Language Models (LLMs). Specifically, this paper examines how Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), combined with commercial product engagement metrics (e.g., Daily Active Users, session retention, user satisfaction ratings), systematically incentivises model "sycophancy"—the tendency of AI models to agree with user premises, fabricate plausible-sounding justifications, and prioritise user appeasement over objective epistemic truth. From a systems safety and regulatory governance perspective, sycophancy represents an unacceptable design flaw that compromises human-in-the-loop oversight and introduces critical failure modes into high-stakes operational environments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Patients increasingly use large language models (LLMs) to understand orthodontic conditions, yet little is known about how leading models compare on the same patient-communication task or how performance varies with the recipient addressed. Methods: In this blinded pilot, five LLMs—Claude (claude-opus-4-7), GPT (gpt-5.5-2026-04-23), Gemini (gemini-2.5-pro), DeepSeek (deepseek-v4-flash), and Grok (grok-4.3)—each explained three orthodontic malocclusions while adopting three clinician personas and addressing three recipient profiles of differing professional background in a complete balanced 5 × 3 × 3 × 3 design (135 responses in Turkish). Three orthodontists independently scored each response on a seven-axis rubric (1–5). Differences used Kruskal–Wallis, Friedman, and Scheirer–Ray–Hare tests with Holm corrections, epsilon-squared effect sizes, and bootstrap confidence intervals. Results: Inter-rater reliability was good (composite ICC [2, 1] = 0.79). Composite scores differed modestly across models (p = 0.044), but no pairwise model difference survived correction; separation was driven by terminology (p = 0.005). Among factors, the recipient profile showed the largest effect size (epsilon-squared = 0.058 vs. 0.045 for model); the engineer profile scored lower than a healthcare worker or layperson (both corrected p < 0.05), with no statistically significant model × recipient interaction detected. Neither persona nor malocclusion affected quality. Conclusions: Because these were prompted profiles and outcomes were expert-rated, deployment and oversight may benefit from attention to audience fit and terminology rather than model choice alone.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as Chat-GPT, Gemini, Claude, Grok and Perplexity have become everyday tools, but the way people actually write is rarely lit-eral.It is packed with slang, memes, idioms, ambiguity and culturespecific phrases whose meaning depends on context and on what speakers already share.Earlier studies mostly looked at these phenomena one at a time, or on only a few models.Here we describe a single, documented framework for comparing current LLMs on real-world language and apply it to 130 expressions drawn from eight categories, including Indian English and Hinglish.Every model got the same prompt, the same four-point rubric and the same error taxonomy, and two human raters scored all 650 responses independently.Accuracy, meaning the share of responses scored 3, was 96.9-98.5% under Rater 1 and 92.3-96.9%un-der Rater 2. The spread between models (1.5 and 4.6 points) is small next to the sampling intervals, while the spread be-tween categories is much wider: memes were weakest (88.0%under Rater 1, 63.0% under Rater 2) and made up 12 of the 15 responses that Rater 1 scored below 3, and cultural mis-understanding was the most frequent error.Only 4 of 650 responses expressed uncertainty, and no model asked a clari-fying question, although the prompt format left little room for one.All five models read all 20 Hinglish and Indian ex-pressions correctly under both raters.The raters agreed on 95.4% of responses (κ = 0.47; Gwet's AC1 = 0.95) and both found memes the weakest category, but they ranked the models differently.

This mixed-methods study compared ChatGPT-generated and teacher-written feedback conditions in university EFL writing and examined how learners perceived the revision value of each condition. A nonrandomized pretest-posttest design was combined with open-ended post-intervention responses. Participants were 46 upper-intermediate learners in a ChatGPT feedback condition ( n = 25) or a teacher-written feedback condition ( n = 21). Across four weeks, both conditions completed the same instructional sequence and two feedback-revision cycles. Writing was scored for task achievement, coherence and cohesion, lexical resource, grammatical accuracy, and an overall composite. Baseline-adjusted models showed a robust difference favoring the ChatGPT condition for overall writing, F(1, 43) = 16.86, p < .001, partial eta squared = 0.282. Unadjusted domain tests favored the ChatGPT condition for task achievement, coherence and cohesion, and lexical resource; after Holm adjustment across the four domains, only task achievement remained below 0.05. Grammatical accuracy did not differ between conditions. Learners described ChatGPT feedback as immediate and elaborated, particularly for content, organization, and vocabulary, while also reporting concerns about trust and contextual fit. Teacher-written feedback was perceived as selective, context-sensitive, and authoritative. The findings support a condition-level advantage in overall writing and suggest different perceived revision affordances, but they do not isolate feedback source from differences in feedback elaboration and immediacy.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The relationship between employee competencies and human factor-related organizational barriers remains understudied. Accordingly, this study examines how technical competencies and soft skills relate to these barriers. A systematic literature review of articles published between 2000 and 2024 and indexed in Scopus and Web of Science was conducted; 77 studies were analyzed. Three key components were identified: technical competencies, soft skills, and organizational properties. The latter may hinder or facilitate the influence of competencies, particularly soft skills, on these barriers. The results show that staff and cultural resistance are closely associated with soft skills, whereas systemic resistance is primarily linked to technical competencies. The study provides an integrative sociotechnical framework for sustainable digital transformation.

An integrative review and evolutionary concept analysis examining how situational awareness is conceptualised, supported, constrained and enacted within acute-care healthcare teams, with particular relevance to simulation-based education. The review synthesises cognitive, behavioural and contextual dimensions of situational awareness to inform simulation design, observation, assessment and debriefing.

We focus on optimisation-based Decision Support Systems in real-world applications. In this context, we aim to provide contrastive explanations that answer users' questions about recommendations based on the solution of an optimisation problem, specifically a Mixed-Integer Program (MIP). Addressing this endeavour is crucial to ensure human oversight of the decisions implemented, as required by international guidelines on trustworthy and responsible automated decision-making systems. We propose a novel methodology that combines constraint reasoning techniques and Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate contrastive explanations for optimisation problems encoded as MIPs. Although LLMs have shown impressive capabilities in Natural Language processing, they can produce incorrect answers due to reasoning limitations. To overcome these limitations, we leverage constraint reasoning techniques to distil the information necessary to produce an explanation, which is then passed as input to an LLM as the so-called graph of reasons. Such a graph captures the semantics and the relationships among constraints of the optimisation problem. Results on real-world scheduling domains show that incorporating constraint reasoning improves explanations generated by the LLM. In particular, using the graph of reasons enables the LLM to produce natural-language explanations that include more relevant reasons while reducing errors compared to explanations generated without this structure.

The article examines contemporary multimedia design in advertising as a complex field of design activity based on the interaction of graphic, audiovisual, dynamic, spatial, and interactive components. The relevance of the study is determined by the spread of digital advertising formats, the increasing complexity of information presentation, and the need to organize technologies, means of artistic expression, and principles of multimedia content development. The research employed the methods of scientific literature analysis, synthesis, comparison, systematization, and classification. The artistic, technological, script-based, communicative, and interactive components of a multimedia advertising product were identified. It was established that the effectiveness of an advertising message depends on the coordination of visual and audio elements, the logic of content development, compositional hierarchy, the suitability of the selected format for audience characteristics, and distribution conditions. Static, dynamic, audiovisual, and interactive advertising formats were compared. Static formats ensure rapid perception of information, dynamic formats guide the sequence of perception, audiovisual formats intensify emotional impact, while interactive formats engage users in active interaction with content. Particular attention was paid to the temporal organization of advertising messages and to the role of movement, rhythm, tempo, editing transitions, music, speech, and sound effects in creating a coherent image. Spatial and immersive technologies were considered as means of extending advertising communication by combining digital objects with the physical environment or by creating an independent virtual space. It was determined that the use of complex technological solutions should be guided by the communication objective, artistic concept, technical capabilities of the platform, and the expected mode of user interaction with the advertising product. The study systematized technologies of two-dimensional graphics, digital typography, motion design, video production, three-dimensional visualization, 3D mapping, augmented and virtual reality, web and mobile interactivity, and artificial intelligence. The means of artistic expression were grouped into visual, dynamic, auditory, spatial, narrative, and interactive categories. The principles of content integrity, compositional hierarchy, audiovisual synchronization, functional dynamics, adaptability, interactive clarity, emotional relevance, information sufficiency, technological appropriateness, and accessibility were substantiated. It was found that excessive animation intensity, visual overload, and inconsistency among media components complicate perception, weaken the emphasis on key information, and reduce communicative expressiveness. The findings confirm that the effectiveness of multimedia advertising is determined not by the number of technologies applied, but by the level of their content-related, compositional, temporal, and functional coordination.

Industrial organizations hold operational knowledge in structured records, such as telemetry, point lists, and transactions, and in unstructured sources, such as manuals, service notes, communications, and inspection reports. Governance programs often manage these sources separately. Classifying, linking, and documenting them depends on a small group of employees with deep domain knowledge. Agents built on large language models can propose metadata, cite documents, and flag quality issues, but unreviewed proposals can spread errors into downstream systems. A perfunctory approval leaves no record of what a reviewer checked. We present contestable governance: specialist agents produce scored, cited arguments for disputed metadata decisions; a steward can accept, reject, modify, or add arguments before commit; and a governance record retains the evidence, interventions, and outcome. A versioned domain glossary supplies model-specific terms and acronym definitions to the agents. We describe the workflow, a triage path that reserves full argumentation for uncertain proposals while preserving review before commit, the scoring and record models, and a gate that controls which verified decisions become precedent. Two HVAC use cases illustrate the pattern: point classification using Brick Schema class labels, supported by an open reference implementation, and an illustrative warranty failure-mode decision linking claim fields and telemetry to service notes and revisioned bulletins.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as experimental subjects in behavioral and economic research. However, it remains unclear whether their decisions reflect stable preferences or context-dependent responses. This study examines intertemporal choice behavior in LLMs within a controlled experimental framework. We implement a fully factorial design across four models (ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, and Claude), varying persona (financially stressed vs. disciplined), delay (1 vs. 6 months), reward magnitude (650–900 $), and prompt framing (direct vs. human-like). Each condition is repeated to approximate response distributions. Results show that LLM behavior is structured but not preference-stable. Decisions are primarily driven by persona conditioning: financially disciplined agents choose delayed rewards significantly more often than stressed agents. Delay and reward magnitude affect choices in line with temporal discounting, while prompt framing has negligible effects. We interpret these findings by conceptualizing LLMs as context-dependent behavioral simulators rather than agents with stable preferences. The contribution is not to establish human equivalence, but to identify the internal consistency and structure of LLM responses under controlled variation. Overall, the results highlight the importance of experimental design and suggest that LLM outputs should be understood as conditional simulations rather than stable expressions of preference.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Reading while walking with smart glasses divides attention between digital text and the surrounding environment, creating a situational impairment. We designed a context-aware alert system using controlled obstacle sensing and nonverbal auditory cues to support partial delegation of environmental monitoring by signaling approaching hazards at two urgency levels. In a controlled outdoor study, 22 participants walked an obstacle course while reading on an augmented reality (AR) headset, with and without alerts. With alerts, reading comprehension scores were higher and participants spent more time looking at the text; walking speed and obstacle clearance did not differ significantly. Exploratory analyses indicated lower perceived physical workload and more positive user experience. Participants appeared to rely more on the system to signal when attention was needed, adopting a more reactive navigation strategy. These results suggest that the alert system enables users to delegate environmental monitoring, freeing attentional resources for reading.

Wrong automatic routing of an IT support ticket can cost more than human triage. We evaluate cost-aware abstention as an offline, cost-conditional readiness assessment: select a routing policy on calibration data under explicit costs, then evaluate that frozen policy once on held-out test data. On a public 47,837-ticket, eight-class corpus, we compare four trained non-LLM classifiers with four large language models under zero- and few-shot prompting. Under the illustrative cost model (c_ok, c_triage, c_wrong) = (0, 1, 5), TF-IDF with logistic regression and a threshold of 0.60 selected on calibration reduces test cost from 0.763 to 0.472, a 38.1% relative reduction (paired ratio-bootstrap 95% CI [35.7%, 40.4%]), while lowering wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%. Frozen calibration-selected policies also beat both always-route and always-defer on held-out test data in 14 of 16 settings in a post-hoc cost-parameter analysis. The strongest prompted configuration reaches 0.477 accuracy on a stratified 1,000-ticket test subset, versus 0.879 for fine-tuned DistilBERT on the same tickets. Isotonic lowers expected calibration error without reliably improving discrimination: GPT-4o-mini few-shot has one confidence value before and after recalibration and correctness AUROC 0.500. We therefore report correctness AUROC and tie-aware risk-coverage area alongside ECE. At the analytically derived break-even probability 0.80, seven prompted configurations defer all tickets; Haiku few-shot routes only 19/1,000. An LLM-only agreement control and margin/entropy rejection baselines further separate calibration from discrimination. The findings are scoped to this dataset, prompt design, model endpoints, and illustrative costs; the work is an evaluation framework, not a new abstention algorithm or universal deployment certification.

Peer review’s reliability on checkable dimensions has been low since the agreement studies of the 1970s and 1980s. The remedies have been known almost as long: explicit criteria, complete rather than sampled checking, and plural independent evaluation. None has been implemented at scale. This paper asks three questions. Is that unreliability a property of human judgment or of procedure? What prevented adoption of the known remedies? And what must an evaluative arrangement satisfy in order to be legitimate? The method is conceptual: the paper synthesizes the empirical literature on peer review with work in social epistemology, procedural legitimacy, and contestable artificial intelligence. It argues for three claims. Reliability on checkable dimensions varies substantially with procedural design. Cost is a necessary but insufficient explanation of non-adoption. And a verdict is legitimate to the degree that it is contestable by the person it burdens; this procedural standard is defended against the epistemic consequentialism that the adjacent literature assumes. On that standard, cheap machine verification changes less than current enthusiasm suggests. Fully specifiable operations, such as statistical recomputation and reference resolution, reach a reliability that human review never approached. Partially specifiable operations gain coverage rather than accuracy. The significance judgment gains nothing. The contribution is a defended standard for judging evaluative institutions, not a case for machine review. The governance and adversarial-robustness conditions that such an arrangement requires are specified, but they are not claimed to be met.

While LLMs have transformed text generation, standard chat-and-canvas interfaces often reduce human authoring to quite passive supervision, causing review fatigue, over-reliance on AI, and the sidelining of the human role in long-form, source-grounded writing. Prior systems typically address isolated writing phases, leaving comprehensive end-to-end human-LLM collaboration largely unexplored. In this paper, we introduce CoWriter, a proactive agentic scheme that adapts expert human (co-)authoring methodologies from cognitive science to flexibly steer the entire writing workflow while actively encouraging the user to engage. In an exploratory user study, compared to a standard LLM baseline, authors using CoWriter better expressed their perspectives and maintained a higher sense of document ownership, supported quantitatively by $2.2\times$ more successful agent engagements. Furthermore, external reader judges rated the resulting texts higher in "human touch" qualities like storytelling and integrating unique personal experiences. Overall, our results demonstrate that proactively engaging users through established human practices is beneficial for effective LLM-supported co-authoring, providing useful methodologies, techniques and insights for future research on collaborative agents.

The 11th of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) explicitly addresses ‘sustainable cities and communities’ and calls for more inclusive, safe and resilient cities (UN 2024 ). Nevertheless, safety and a feeling of security are often neglected in urban development, with the design and functional aspects more frequently in focus. At the same time, crime in general, as well as crime that occurs in public spaces, is constantly on the rise (Vykopalová 2021 ). In this context, this paper examines whether and how artificial intelligence (AI) in university planning education can contribute to making public spaces safer. The challenges and potential of artificial intelligence in university teaching are discussed through a case study of the Raschplatz, a semi-public space at the central train station in Hanover (Lower Saxony). Over the course of a project from 2023 to 2025, students from the Faculty of Architecture and Landscape Sciences at Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz University Hanover photographed situations at the Raschplatz where they felt safe or unsafe and conducted a brief survey among the users of the area. The survey asked 270 users how often they visited the Raschplatz and why, how long they typically stayed in the area, and how safe they felt there, among other things. The students used these results to create visualisations of crime prevention measures with and without the Dall-E 2 AI text-to-image model. The study examines the extent to which spatial planning and AI can contribute to the development of measures that enhance the feeling of safety in public spaces, and demonstrates how and where planning and AI can benefit from each other. Through the case study of the Raschplatz, the paper critically reflects on how AI (tools) can help enhance sustainable and innovative teaching. It demonstrates that AI-generated visualisations can effectively illustrate potential measures; however, it also highlights the apparent limitations of using AI to prevent crime through urban or environmental planning. For example, AI’s visualisation of those measures is often technically accurate, but not well suited to the existing spatial structures. AI can help increase students’ interest in task processing and prompt reflection, and contribute to controversial debates in university teaching.

Given differences in the associative memory architectures of humans and AI, it is not clear whether AI generates and interprets visual-linguistic associations the way humans do. To investigate this, human participants and two large language models (LLMs), ChatGPT and Gemini, were asked to generate novel words and corresponding images that form meaningfully linked dyads. The LLMs and a second group of human participants were presented with shuffled sets of these words and images and asked to rematch them in ways they felt were most meaningful. Humans performed similarly regardless of whether the pairs were human or LLM-generated, while LLMs were better at matching LLM-generated pairs. Overall, LLMs outperformed humans at recovering the intended pairings. These findings suggest that despite architectural differences, the way in which AI generates and detects associations between language and visual stimuli is not only like that of humans, but they may be superior at recognizing cross-domain associations that humans find meaningful.

This study examines whether interactions with trained interpreters using empathy-focused messaging through the Seattle Aquarium Beach Naturalist Program are associated with higher levels of empathy toward marine life. Empathy-focused messaging included perspective-taking, relational and anthropomorphic framing, individualization, and narrative storytelling designed to encourage visitors to consider the experiences of intertidal organisms. The study specifically emphasized less charismatic intertidal animals that are less likely to elicit immediate affective engagement, including organisms without readily discernable faces or eyes. Drawing on three summers of survey data (2023–2025) (n = 263) from beaches in the Pacific Northwest of the US, we assess affective and cognitive empathy among individuals who did and did not interact with a naturalist during a low-tide event. Respondents completed surveys with Likert and open-ended questions about empathy, what they learned, and how the experience might influence future behavior. Results indicate that encounters with trained interpreters using empathy-focused messaging are associated with increased empathy toward intertidal marine life. Qualitative analysis of open-ended questions further shows that interactions are correlated with heightened awareness, stewardship and protection, animal-centered perspective shifts, and learning and knowledge sharing regarding shoreline ecosystems. These findings suggest that beach naturalist programming with empathy-focused messaging could strengthen both emotional and cognitive engagement with intertidal organisms while fostering more conservation-oriented behavior intentions. These results are relevant to scholars of environmental education and human–animal studies, as well as aquariums, parks departments, conservation organizations, and community-based educators seeking to promote more informed, empathetic, and protective engagement among residents and visitors in coastal environments.

Neutrino telescopes record more than a trillion photon detections per year, yet there does not exist a self-supervised learning (SSL) task which fully satisfies all three conditions: improving as the pretraining set grows, transferring to a different detector, and outperforming the best model trained without pretraining at all. We introduce CURTAIN, a temporal masking scheme and the first SSL task for neutrino telescopes that achieves all of these goals. Downstream performance monotonically improves with the number of pretraining events, as predicted by scaling laws. Our encoder builds on DeepIce, currently the leading model on the NuBench benchmarks direction reconstruction task. Pretraining it with CURTAIN reduces its median angular error by 45% and its median energy error by 31% compared to training from scratch. It also transfers to a detector geometry never seen in pretraining, reducing the median angular error by 36% compared to training from scratch. At matched capacity and pretraining data, CURTAIN-pretrained encoders beat those pretrained by existing SSL tasks on both tasks and at every pretraining set size.

Drought affects more than 60% of India's population, reducing agricultural productivity, straining water resources, and threatening socioeconomic stability. This study proposes an interpretable one-month-ahead meteorological drought prediction framework by integrating class-weighted ensemble machine learning with SHAP and LIME explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Historical meteorological observations (1972–2022) obtained from the Zenodo climate database were analyzed for 49 districts across five drought-prone Indian states (Bihar, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, and Karnataka). After generating lagged meteorological features (t − 1 to t − 6) and addressing severe class imbalance (7.07% drought events), multiple machine learning classifiers were evaluated. The class-weighted XGBoost model (scale_pos_weight ≈ 11.90, without SMOTE) achieved the best overall performance on the independent 2016–2022 test dataset, with an accuracy of 95.7%, macro precision of 84.7%, macro recall of 81.0%, macro F1-score of 82.7%, and a PR-AUC of 0.647 on the highly imbalanced test set (outperforming both unweighted training and SMOTE-based approaches). SHAP and LIME consistently identified lagged Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI), lagged precipitation, vapour pressure, and wet-day frequency as the most influential drivers of drought occurrence. Exploratory temporal analysis further revealed declining wet-day frequency in Karnataka, increasing vapour pressure in Andhra Pradesh, and substantial climatic variability across the study regions. The proposed framework combines accurate drought prediction with transparent model interpretation, providing a practical decision-support tool for district-level drought early warning, water resource management, and climate-resilient agricultural planning in India.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) are reshaping cybersecurity, moving it from signature-based reactive security to agentic, self-evolving, and proactive operations. However, the fast deployment of autonomous agents entails significant security issues, physical-layer attacks in cyber-physical systems, alignment problems, and advanced social engineering risks jeopardizing the stability of the modern sociotechnical infrastructures. This survey paper, which summarizes and analyses the literature, examines the duality of AI in cybersecurity, exploring its implications for strengthening digital defences and increasing the threat landscape for adversaries. We perform a thorough review of 36 cutting-edge research articles, which are organized into six important areas: self-evolving defensive paradigms, LLM-based intelligent agents, reinforcement learning for autonomous decision-making, security of cyber-physical systems, human-machine co-teaming, and agent alignment. Our synthesis shows that multi-agent collaborations greatly shorten incident response times and automate discovery of vulnerabilities but are also highly vulnerable to prompt injection, training data poisoning, and physical-layer spoofing. Moreover, we identify a shift from model patches to model alignment and constitutional safety at runtime as a prerequisite for securing these systems. We believe that resilient digital defence must also be considered a sociotechnical problem, as there must be agents, autonomous systems, that are governed by other agents, aligned and constitutionally bound, and are able to collaborate, rather than operate completely separately, with human operators.

To provide personalized learning experiences in courses that teach data analysis skills, instructors often search for datasets that appeal to a student's interests, align with specific learning objectives, and are appropriate for the student's skill level. Datasets that match all three criteria can be difficult to find. DagFlow-AI is an agentic AI data generation tool that creates realistic, synthetic datasets tailored to these criteria. Rather than mimicking existing datasets or generating observations directly, DagFlow-AI uses the broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to specify the components of transparent, reproducible data-generating mechanisms from which observations are generated programmatically. We illustrate how the tool can be used to construct a realistic, synthetic dataset and describe how it aligns with both the Guidelines for Assessment and Instruction of Statistics Education (GAISE) and the Problem, Plan, Data, Analysis, and Conclusion (PPDAC) framework for teaching data analysis

The article examines the role of data analysis methods in modern management and their integration with anti-corruption mechanisms, integrity principles, and professional communication in the Ukrainian business environment. The relevance of the study is determined by the rapid digitalization of economic processes, the growing volume and diversity of available information, increasing market competition, and the need to ensure the speed, validity, transparency, and accountability of managerial decision-making. The study substantiates the transformation of traditional management approaches toward data-driven management, in which data are considered a strategic resource for achieving organizational goals and developing sustainable competitive advantages. Particular attention is paid to comparative, correlation, regression, and factor analysis, as well as econometric modeling and modern analytical technologies, including Business Intelligence, Big Data, Predictive Analytics, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. Their potential for monitoring key performance indicators, identifying trends and anomalies, forecasting changes, assessing risks, optimizing business processes, and supporting evidence-based managerial decisions is determined. The article also considers the role of data analysis in strengthening organizational integrity and preventing corruption. Digital monitoring, automated control procedures, anomaly detection, and analytical processing of large datasets can contribute to identifying potential corruption risks and increasing the transparency and accountability of management processes. At the same time, it is emphasized that technological tools cannot independently guarantee integrity, since their effectiveness depends on data quality, transparency of procedures, ethical standards, professional competence, and responsibility for managerial decisions. The study further highlights the importance of professional communication as a link between analytical justification and practical implementation of management decisions. Clear, logical, structured, and accurate communication in Ukrainian contributes to the proper interpretation of analytical results, coordination of organizational actions, accountability, and effective implementation of decisions. The study proposes an integrated approach that combines data analysis, integrity, and professional communication as interrelated components of modern management. Data analysis provides analytical validity, integrity ensures transparency, ethics, and accountability, while professional communication ensures accurate understanding and effective practical implementation of managerial decisions. The proposed approach can serve as a basis for further development of responsible, transparent, data-driven management practices in the Ukrainian business environment.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being frequently applied in information organizations for the attainment of innovative outcomes. With the rapid incorporation of GenAI in information based organizations, the need of effective data governance has become a vital need of the current age. GenAI systems rely on huge and diverse datasets that include user generated content, metadata, big data, organizational documentation, research data, and public sources. Hence, gaps in data governance can have a negative impact on the reliability, validity, accuracy, security, confidentiality, privacy, and responsible use of GenAI. Effective data governance is necessary to ensure data accuracy to protect sensitive information for addressing copyright issues.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Ensuring privacy in digital ecosystems presents significant challenges. Individual privacy-related decision-making has been widely criticised as insufficient. The mobility context, where computing is typically ubiquitous, makes this type of decision-making also operationally infeasible. This study examines whether innovative data governance strategies offer a promising approach. Drawing on contextual integrity theory, this paper examines the perceived appropriateness of delegating privacy-related decision-making to different types of data intermediaries (data cooperatives, AI agents, and experts) in mobility contexts. Specifically, a stratified, full-factorial vignette study ( N = 600) is conducted. The vignettes systematically varied across four contextual factors: sender, information type, purpose, and duration of data access approval. This design allows for the examination of how contextual factors influence preferences for data intermediary-based decision-making in mobility settings. Findings show that scenarios in which data cooperatives acted as the decision-makers were consistently rated as more appropriate than those involving AI agents or experts, particularly in high-stakes contexts such as traffic management and ambulance coordination. Nevertheless, scenarios involving individual control received the highest overall appropriateness ratings. Respondents’ preferences were context-dependent: they showed greater acceptance when the purpose of sharing aligned with public benefit, and when the access duration was either short (e.g., one day) or revocable (e.g., ‘until revoked’). The results underscore the relevance of hybrid governance models that combine individual control with the ability to delegate decision-making to trusted intermediaries, particularly in mobility contexts. Together, these contributions could aid in developing context-sensitive privacy frameworks that align with societal values in ubiquitous computing environments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Precisely deconstructing the numerical composition of advertising cost‐conversion efficiency (ACTE) and uncovering its microlevel associative mechanisms are critical for enterprises to optimize marketing decisions. To overcome the limitations of existing methods regarding modeling accuracy and result interpretability, this study constructs an analytical framework integrating machine learning with interpretable artificial intelligence. Using 174,584 real‐world microlevel advertising records from a Chinese telecommunications company in July 2024, we systematically compared six representative machine learning models, rigorously evaluating them against a historical average baseline. The findings reveal that the XGBoost model achieves optimal fitting and generalization performance, with a test set coefficient of determination of 0.8236 ± 0.2061, significantly outperforming the baseline and other models. Furthermore, SHAP‐based interpretability analysis not only precisely quantifies the contribution of each feature to the ACTE value but also systematically reveals underlying nonlinear dependencies and threshold effects. Specifically, the advertising conversion rate plays a dominant role; exposure frequency shows a step‐like positive association; production cost exhibits a reversal effect demarcated by the median; click‐through rate and play volume display discrete stratified structures; and average display cost contributes minimally. Specification tests indicate that ACTE interpretability primarily stems from algebraic relationships of constitutive features, with limited independent contributions from non‐constitutive features. Theoretically, this study provides microlevel evidence for nonlinear advertising associations; methodologically, it establishes a rigorous modeling‐to‐interpretation paradigm; and practically, it offers empirically grounded decision support for advertising exposure regulation and cost optimization.

The recent developments in artificial intelligence have had a significant influence on drug discovery, with the possibility of modeling drug-like molecules based on data. Graph neural networks and other deep learning methods have been shown to be effective for learning useful molecular representations, as well as for learning complex chemical structures directly based on data. The chapter offers an introduction to deep learning analysis through the focus on graph-based algorithms of the prediction of molecular properties, drug-likeness, and de novo generation of molecules. It talks about prominent molecular representations like SMILES, molecular fingerprints, and molecular graphs, and how they are incorporated into the current neural network models. The chapter also examines evaluation metrics and reports real-world research on the usefulness of these models in practical drug discovery. Lastly, it outlines the existing constraints, research gaps, and challenges in the future, insisting on the increased use of deep learning and GNNs in pharmaceutical discovery speeds and improvements.

Abstract Histological grading of urothelial carcinoma is subject to interobserver variability. We evaluated whether artificial intelligence (AI)-based whole-slide mitotic quantification provides an objective adjunct to histological grading. We developed and validated a deep learning-based mitotic detection framework trained on 91,183 patches with 318,893 annotations. A multi-reader crossover study was conducted in internal ( n = 149) and external ( n = 316) cohorts, where three independent pathologists graded cases in unassisted and model-assisted phases. In the combined cohort ( n = 465), AI-derived mitotic count showed high diagnostic accuracy for high-grade carcinoma (area under the curve [AUC] 0.91, 95% CI 0.89–0.94) at a cut-off of 17.5 mitoses per 2 mm². AI assistance significantly improved mean reader AUC from 0.90 to 0.98 in the internal cohort ( p = 0.038). In the external cohort, the mean reader AUC increased from 0.84 to 0.95, although this difference did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.11). AI assistance also significantly reduced interobserver variability (Fleiss’s κ: 0.72 to 0.93 internally; 0.62 to 0.85 externally; both, p < 0.001). AI-based mitotic quantification provides an objective and standardized adjunct to histological grading and reduces interobserver variability. This approach may improve diagnostic accuracy and support clinical decision-making, pending prospective validation.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Occupational exoskeletons promise significant reductions in worker physical burden and injury risk, yet industrial adoption rates remain low despite positive laboratory performance data. This persistent gap between demonstrated efficacy and actual deployment suggests that unmeasured barriers beyond task-performance metrics may influence adoption decisions. We examined whether pre- and post-use tasks generate usability problems that could act as barriers to adoption. Seven evaluators trained in human factors and heuristic evaluation evalauted three passive exoskeletons representing different support mechanisms: a shoulder-support device (Skelex), a lumbar-support device (Laevo), and a sit-stand support device (Chairless Chair). Using a combined framework of Nielsen usability heuristics and Shneiderman principles adapted for physical wearable systems, evaluators independently identified usability problems across all four deployment task phases, rated problem severity on a 5-point scale, and participated in structured reconciliation discussions to resolve rating divergences. Evaluators identified 158 usability problems across the three devices, 62 of which were rated as major problems (mean severity at or above 2.5): 29 for the shoulder-support, 15 for the back-support, and 18 for the sit-stand exoskeleton. Assembly accounted for 46% of the heuristic violations associated with major problems (114 of 250), ranging from 41% to 54% across devices. Agreement among the independent severity ratings was moderate for the seven-evaluator mean (ICC(2,7) = 0.67). Because the study did not measure adoption, these problems are plausible barriers to adoption that warrant field investigation. Six problem categories recurred across devices regardless of support mechanism, four of them in all three devices: two-person operation requirements (severity 2.9-3.1), poor documentation (severity 3.0), absent sequence indicators (severity 2.6-2.9), manual strength barriers (severity 2.7-3.1), universal design violations (severity 2.6–3.4), and hazards and safety problems, which included component ricochet on the shoulder-support device (severity 3.3–3.4), fall risk on the sit-stand device (severity 2.6–2.7), and pinch points on both.
