Objective This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to synthesize the results of randomized controlled trials to determine whether medication management approaches based on digital technologies and artificial intelligence/machine learning can indeed bring measurable clinical improvements in older adults with at least one chronic diseases. Methods To identify relevant RCTs, we performed a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, CNKI, Wanfang, and other databases from their inception through June 30, 2026, for studies of digital and AI/ML-based medication management in older adults with at least one chronic diseases. All stages of study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment were conducted independently by two reviewers, applying the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool. Meta-analytic pooling was conducted via RevMan 5.4. Results Nineteen RCTs met the inclusion criteria, of which 6 were included in the meta-analysis and 13 in the descriptive synthesis. For medication adherence, three studies reported highly heterogeneous results ( I 2 = 97%), and because of this heterogeneity and the small number of studies, the data were not pooled; the individual study estimates ranged from SMD = −0.28–SMD = 1.89. For PIMs, only one study reported a comparable outcome; no pooled estimate was calculated. For hospitalization and mortality, the two included studies used different effect measures (HR and OR) and were therefore presented separately: Blum et al. reported an HR of 0.95 (95% CI 0.77–1.17), and Rieckert et al. reported an OR of 0.88 (95% CI 0.73–1.07). Conclusion The current body of evidence does not establish clinically meaningful benefits of digital or AI/ML-based medication management on hard endpoints such as hospitalization and mortality among older adults with at least one chronic diseases. For medication adherence, the evidence remains inconclusive and highly heterogeneous, and no reliable pooled estimate could be obtained. Given the pronounced heterogeneity and the limited pool of high-quality RCTs, current evidence is insufficient to establish clinical benefit for the routine implementation of digital or AI/ML-based medication management systems in geriatric care and further rigorously designed studies are warranted. Systematic review registration CRD420261460445.

The fast growth of digital technology in financial systems has changed the nature of financial fraud. This has created new problems for traditional methods of accounting, auditing and investigation. Because of this, digital forensic accounting has become more important. It is a multidisciplinary approach that combines accounting knowledge, investigative methods, digital forensics and advanced technologies. This study examines the role of digital forensic accounting in fraud detection, financial investigation and financial integrity. It uses a conceptual and narrative review of academic literature, professional reports and reliable sources. The review shows that digital evidence, data analytics, artificial intelligence and machine learning can help identify suspicious transactions. These tools can also help examine financial data and trace financial activities. Digital forensic accounting supports fraud prevention, internal controls, transparency, accountability and corporate governance. However, technological complexity, privacy concerns, legal and ethical issues and the need for specialised skills remain important challenges.

Digital health and artificial intelligence are becoming influential in shaping global health policy due to the opportunities they will offer in improving access, efficiency and health outcomes globally. At the same time, such technologies spark critical issues regarding inequality, ethics, and governance-especially in developing countries in low-income and middle-income countries. This chapter focuses on how digital health and AI are changing the global health systems and just how both these can have a positive effect or a threat towards those who might not have access to usable technology or AI. It examines policy issues concerning governance, regulation, and human rights and the role of international collaboration when working towards equitable and responsible adoption of health technologies using artificial intelligence.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The Internet and artificial intelligence (AI) have become deeply embedded in contemporary education, research and professional life. Their capacity to enhance learning efficiency and reduce access costs is undeniable. Yet these technologies have also generated significant negative externalities: students are increasingly distanced from printed textbooks and library-based study, turning instead to instantly available digital resources and generative AI tools. This shift has contributed to the erosion of deep reading, critical thinking and creativity. Drawing on recent empirical evidence, this article analyses the mechanisms through which screen-based reading and AI dependence undermine cognitive development, and argues that educational institutions must intervene through formal rules and regulations to minimise these externalities. It proposes a policy framework centred on the principle of preserving cognitive friction, encompassing curriculum design, pedagogical norms and assessment reform.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter examines how Industry 4.0 technologies reshape servitization and service-oriented manufacturing within digitally transforming supply chains. While digital servitization is often associated with technologies such as IoT, artificial intelligence, cloud platforms, analytics, and digital twins, the chapter argues that technology adoption alone is insufficient to generate service-oriented performance. Drawing on service-dominant logic, business model innovation, supply chain integration, socio-technical systems thinking, and dynamic capabilities theory, the chapter develops a theory-informed model explaining how manufacturers sense digital service opportunities, seize them through Industry 4.0-enabled service offerings, and reconfigure supply chain relationships around lifecycle value creation. The model is applied to an anonymous industrial equipment manufacturing case that illustrates the transition from product sales and reactive maintenance toward predictive maintenance, remote diagnostics, lifecycle service agreements, and recurring service revenue. The chapter contributes by positioning digital servitization as a capability-driven supply chain transformation and highlights practical conditions related to data governance, supplier readiness, customer trust, cybersecurity, and service-oriented performance measurement.

The accelerating digitisation of higher education has prompted urgent questions about which technology-mediated pedagogical interventions most effectively improve student learning outcomes in scientific disciplines. Drawing on a cross-institutional survey of 1500 undergraduate and postgraduate students enrolled in STEM and scientific programmes across five institution types, this study investigates the individual and joint effects of three canonical digital transformation mechanisms: virtual simulation laboratories (VSL), artificial intelligence-assisted learning (AIAAL), and blended teaching models (BTM). Employing a mixed-methods empirical framework that combines structural equation modelling (SEM), multi-level fixed-effects regression, and bootstrap mediation analysis, we estimate standardised direct effects of 0.264, 0.218, and 0.192 for VSL, AIAAL, and BTM on academic achievement, respectively. Mediation analysis reveals that self-regulated learning (SRL), collaborative knowledge construction, and cognitive engagement jointly channel 55.5% of the VSL effect and 54.7% of the AIAAL effect through indirect pathways, underscoring the primacy of process-level learning mechanisms. Moderation analysis demonstrates that institutional readiness amplifies all three technology effects by 42-68%, while disciplinary context generates the sharpest differential: VSL effects in STEM disciplines are 110% larger than in non-STEM contexts, whereas AIAAL effects remain comparably robust across disciplines. Robustness tests using instrumental variables, propensity score matching, and difference-in-differences quasi-experimental designs confirm that results are not artefacts of selection bias or omitted variable contamination. Policy scenario projections to 2030 suggest that full digital integration could reduce inter-institutional achievement gaps by 74% relative to business-as-usual. The findings contribute a theoretically grounded and empirically validated framework for evidence-based digital transformation in scientific higher education.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is now a crucial element in the transforming of industries globally, propelled by greater development in computational processing, cloud and computational services, and deep learning technologies. Its uses, ranging from chatbots to self-driving cars, are becoming more widespread, presenting the opportunity to enhance organizational efficiency by as much as 40%. In light of global competitiveness and digital transformation, which have been induced by the COVID-19 era, AI is crucial, especially for Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs). Nevertheless, SMEs face considerable obstacles to AI acceptance, such as financial and technical limitations, restricted access to advanced technologies, and a shortage of skilled personnel. These issues hinder their productivity and competitiveness within the national economy. This research investigates the elements that affect AI acceptance in the landscape of SMEs in Gauteng, with the goal of identifying barriers, evaluating the impact of managerial leadership, and assessing the use of AI in operations. A sample of 118 stakeholders, including owners, managers, and strategic employees from various backgrounds, was analysed, excluding large corporations and government entities. The study focuses on the ICT sector, exploring technological, organizational, environmental, and ethical aspects of AI implementation. The capstone report aims to formulate strategies that assist SMEs in overcoming challenges related to digital transformation, offering an introduction, literature review, methodology, analysis, and strategic recommendations specifically designed for the South African context. This research demonstrates that AI adoption among Gauteng's SMEs stands at a critical inflection point. Strong awareness of AI's potential combines with substantial adoption intentions, creating conditions for rapid diffusion. However, realising this potential requires coordinated action addressing identified barriers through organisational capability building, ecosystem enablement, and supportive policy frameworks. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Technology, Environment, Organisation, SMEs
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The growing demand for personalized drug delivery necessitates intelligent computational approaches that can jointly analyze molecular characteristics, biological targets, physicochemical properties, and therapeutic responses.This study presents a Digital Twin-Assisted Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network (PI-GNN) integrated with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to facilitate drug-target response prediction and personalized therapeutic optimization.The proposed framework was developed using 52,274 drug-target interaction records, partitioned into 36,592 training, 5,227 validation, and 10,455 testing samples.Molecular structures were transformed into graphs characterized by 23 atom-level and six bond-level features, while protein sequences were represented through 24 biological attributes.Eight physicochemical parameters-molecular weight, LogP, topological polar surface area (TPSA), hydrogen-bond donors, hydrogen-bond acceptors, rotatable bonds, ring count, and fraction Csp3-were incorporated to provide physics-informed constraints to the learning process.Experimental evaluation on the log-transformed response yielded an R² of 0.4209, RMSE of 2.2985, and MAE of 1.5695 for the test dataset.Permutation-based XAI revealed TPSA as the dominant physicochemical contributor, with its perturbation increasing RMSE by 0.1662 and decreasing R² by 0.0868, followed by molecular weight, LogP, ring count, and hydrogen-bond donors.Molecular-level interpretability was further established using GNNExplainer to identify influential atoms associated with individual predictions.Input-ablation analysis showed that suppressing physicochemical and protein information reduced R² from 0.4209 to -5.0589 and 0.3276, respectively, indicating that the trained network relied substantially on these complementary information sources.The XAI-guided digital-twin module evaluated 10,661 valid molecular candidates, with 5,756 satisfying the specified drug-like constraints.For the selected biological target context, Drug ID 1049 was identified as the highest-ranked candidate, increasing the predicted log-response from 8.5935 to 15.5521, representing an 80.98% relative improvement on the modelled log-response scale and achieving a digital-twin score of 0.8905.Overall, the findings indicate that combining graph-based molecular learning with physicochemical knowledge, model explainability, and digital-twin-driven candidate screening offers an interpretable computational strategy for prioritizing promising drug-target configurations.The framework provides a foundation for subsequent experimental validation and the development of data-driven personalized drug-delivery systems.

I denne artikkelen undersøker forfatterne kjennetegn ved barnehager i Norge som benytter digital teknologi når de leser sammen med barna i barnehagen. Målet med studien er å få økt kunnskap om barnehagens digitale lesepraksis, hvorvidt den faktisk eksisterer, og hva som i så fall kjennetegner barnehager som har denne praksisen. Nasjonale styringsdokumenter legger stor vekt på at all bruk av digital teknologi sammen med barn i barnehagen skal ha høy pedagogisk kvalitet. Studien er multimetodisk og består av kvantitative data fra en nasjonal spørreundersøkelse (N = 1192) og kvalitative data fra dybdeintervju med to barnehagelærere som leser digitale bøker sammen med barna i barnehagen. Funn fra spørreundersøkelsen viser at digital lesing ikke er en utbredt del av norske barnehagers lesepraksiser. Funnene viser også at det som kjennetegner de barnehagene som har en digital lesepraksis, er at de har enkeltpersoner i personalgruppen med en indre motivasjon for å lese digitale bøker, og som tilsynelatende er alene om å drive og opprettholde den digitale lesepraksisen. Disse personene leser digitale bøker til tross for at de også uttrykker stor frustrasjon over både dårlig tilgang til interessante digitale bøker på norsk og manglende tilgang til digital teknologi. ENGLISH ABSTRACT Digital reading practices i Norwegian kindergartens In this article, the authors explore the characteristics of kindergartens in Norway that incorporate digital technology into their reading practices with children. The aim of the study is to deepen our understanding of digital reading practices in kindergartens—whether such practices are present, and if so, what characterises kindergartens with this practice. National policy documents emphasize that all use of digital technology in kindergartens must uphold high pedagogical quality. The study employs a multi-methodical approach, combining quantitative data from a national survey (N = 1192) and qualitative data from in-depth interviews with two kindergarten teachers who read digital books with the children in kindergarten. Findings from the survey indicate that digital reading is generally not integrated into Norwegian kindergartens’ reading practices. However, in kindergartens where digital reading does occur, it is typically driven by individual teachers who possess a strong intrinsic motivation to use digital books. These individuals often operate in isolation, sustaining the digital reading practice despite expressing significant frustration over limited access to engaging digital books in Norwegian and limited access to digital technology.

Background: The professional development of higher vocational college teachers is shaped not only by individual competence but also by the relationships among colleges, industry partners, policy systems, digital resources, and regional conditions. In Inner Mongolia, a useful analytical approach must account for both the common pressures of vocational education and the region’s diverse economic and geographic settings. Aim: This paper examines key dilemmas affecting teacher professional development and proposes an ecology-oriented framework for improvement. Methodology: It adopts a conceptual, literature-based analysis of the four Chinese studies supplied for this paper, supplemented by a contextual review of publicly available material on vocational education and teacher development in the region. It does not claim to report original survey or interview data. Findings: The analysis identifies five connected challenges: an insufficiently differentiated professional role, uneven access to authentic workplace learning, fragmented institutional support, a gap between digital tools and pedagogical application, and evaluation mechanisms that may privilege visible outputs over sustained growth. These challenges are interpreted through the ecological concepts of niche, interaction, limiting factors, and the “flowerpot effect.” Conclusion: Sustainable improvement requires coordinated action at teacher, college, industry, and regional-policy levels. The paper recommends differentiated development pathways, long-term school–enterprise learning communities, practice-oriented digital development, more supportive evaluation, and regionally responsive resource sharing. These proposals should be tested through empirical research in representative institutions across Inner Mongolia.

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong potential to automate heuristic design for NP-hard combinatorial optimization (CO) tasks without human intervention. Recent methods predominantly rely on evolutionary computation (EC) frameworks, where heuristic diversification is mainly induced through EC-like operators or downstream selection, while the direction of heuristic transformation remains largely unharnessed. In this paper, we propose a multi-directional Perturbation-Rewrite Search (PRS) framework for automatic heuristic design that factorizes heuristic transformation through directional search primitives at the generation level. Specifically, PRS operates on heuristic ideas through three complementary directions: expansion toward richer and more expressive designs, compression toward simpler and less specialized designs, and steering for fine-grained refinement, together enabling broader and more sustained exploration of diverse regions in the heuristic design space. PRS further organizes candidate exploration within a breadth-first search-based process with adaptive operator control, which ensures thorough candidate utilization and sustained exploration, and maintains strong search dynamics while preventing premature convergence. Extensive empirical results across diverse CO tasks show that PRS consistently discovers high-quality heuristics, demonstrating the effectiveness and generality of explicitly directional exploration design.

This study investigates the realisation and interactional functions of directive speech acts in researcher–AI communication through a reflexive case study of an academic journal submission. While directive speech acts have been extensively examined in human–human institutional interactions, limited empirical attention has been paid to how directives are constructed and deployed when the addressee is an artificial intelligence (AI) system operating within digitally mediated academic workflows. As AI systems increasingly assist scholars in writing and navigating editorial platforms, it is necessary to examine how action, authority, and epistemic responsibility are negotiated in human–AI interactions. This study addresses this gap by analysing a naturally occurring dialogue between a researcher and ChatGPT during the real-time submission of a manuscript to an international Q1 journal. The dataset comprised a complete 46-turn interaction sequence, from which 16 researcher-initiated directive moves were identified as primary units of analysis. Adopting a qualitative reflexive case study design, the analysis draws on speech act theory (Searle, 1976), interactional epistemics (Heritage, 2012), and relational work (Locher & Watts, 2008) to examine the linguistic realisation and functional deployment of directives across submission stages. The findings reveal that directives are predominantly realised through interrogative constructions rather than bald imperatives. WH-questions (e.g., “What should I do?”) and yes/no interrogatives pragmatically function as action-eliciting moves, particularly at moments of procedural uncertainty. These interrogatives enable the researcher to seek guidance while mitigating imposition, constructing AI as a procedural authority without an overt command. In addition to interrogatives, mitigated imperatives (e.g. “please explain”) and declarative problem reports (e.g., “I clicked OK, but there is no response”) operate as directive resources, demonstrating that directive force is interactionally achieved rather than strictly encoded in the grammatical mood. Functionally, four directive categories emerged: procedural guidance, explanatory mediation, confirmation for epistemic risk management, and evaluative positioning. Procedural guidance directives are clustered during technically opaque stages, such as PDF generation and final approval. Explanatory directives seek clarification of institutional prompts, positioning AI as an interpretive mediator. Confirmation directives appear before irreversible actions, reflecting heightened epistemic caution. A smaller subset of evaluative directives solicits normative stances regarding open-access decisions, extending human–AI interaction into moral reasoning. Directive density increases in phases characterised by institutional opacity, suggesting a correlation between procedural risks and directive production. Notably, directives are consistently mitigated through relational address terms and politeness markers despite the AI’s nonhuman status. This persistence of mitigation indicates that relational framing may function as a routinised communicative schema rather than solely as a face-protecting adjustment. Overall, this study argues that directives in researcher–AI interactions operate as mechanisms of institutional navigation and epistemic regulation rather than coercive command structures, contributing to empirical insights into the emerging field of human–AI pragmatics.

The growth of time-series datasets and foundation models has made dataset comparison a central part of time-series workflows. Assessing source-target transfer before model adaptation requires similarity estimates that can summarize transfer-related dataset relationships without exhaustive source-target evaluation over every candidate pair. Many metrics have been proposed for measuring similarity between time-series datasets, but they capture different dataset relationships and vary in how well they align with downstream utility across tasks. We evaluate this gap by measuring the correlation between source-target similarity scores and downstream forecasting errors in out-of-distribution and transfer-learning settings. We propose Domain-Integrated Similarity Cost (DISC), a learnable aggregation framework that uses calibration transfer observations to select, weight, and combine similarity metrics for different downstream tasks. By integrating complementary metric values, DISC better distinguishes source-target dataset differences that matter for downstream behavior. After calibration, DISC scores source-target pairs using only their similarity-metric values and yields higher alignment than single-metric references on the reported split. These results show that time-series dataset similarity is task-dependent, and that learned metric integration provides a stronger proxy for downstream transfer behavior than manually selecting one similarity metric.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Respect for religious diversity creates a welcoming hotel environment, benefiting guests, staff, and the business’s overall performance. Anchored in the theory of planned behavior (TPB), this study examines the relationships between implementation of religious diversity management practices (RDMPs), employee engagement, staff intention to continue working in a hotel, and the moderating role of ethical leadership. This research employs a quantitative design, gathering data through a survey of 522 employees in the Egyptian hotel sector. The results indicate that RDMPs exert a beneficial impact on both employee engagement and the intention to remain. Ethical leadership also acts as a moderator on the relationships between RDMPs and physical engagement, RDMPs and emotional engagement, and RDMPs and cognitive engagement. Hoteliers should provide training that demonstrate the importance of RDMPs to managers and staff. Recognition of employees’ religious beliefs can include considering nutritional requirements and religious holidays. Leaders who model ethical behavior can have a significant impact on how RDMPs are implemented, aiding in the development of a work culture of mutual respect and trust. The research provides new directions in studying the management of religious diversity, particularly in the Global South and Muslim-majority countries.

Accurate State of Health (SOH) estimation is essential for ensuring the safety, reliability, and long-term performance of electric vehicle batteries. However, the generalization performance of Artificial Intelligence methods depends on the quality and coverage of training data. Acquiring high-quality labeled data with sufficient coverage remains a challenge. To address this, this paper first comprehensively compares and analyzes the State of Charge (SOC) dependence of the mechanical, electrical, and thermal features of batteries under different initial SOC. Features with weak SOC dependence are selected as model inputs, enabling robust SOH estimation in partial charge–discharge scenarios using only fully completed charge–discharge data. This effectively reduces the model’s demand for broad data coverage. Then, this paper proposes a domain adaptation method based on Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), which integrates the Transformer and Kolmogorov–Arnold Network (KAN). Experimental results show that adopting features with weak SOC dependence reduces the relative Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) by 85.48% for slow charging and 64.33% for fast charging. Moreover, the proposed domain adaptation method achieves a 47.69% relative reduction in MAPE.

Recent advances in speech generation are shifting toward context-aware, multi-turn, and multi-speaker synthesis. While these capabilities are in high demand for applications such as audiobook and audio drama production, evaluation has not kept pace with these advances. Beyond traditional zero-shot Text-to-Speech (TTS), modern systems in this domain primarily fall into three categories: instruction-controllable generation models, multi-turn dialogue models, and the audio branches of audio-visual generation models. However, existing benchmarks evaluate these paradigms in isolation, failing to provide a unified assessment of context modeling, instruction following, and multi-speaker generation. Meanwhile, recent progress in audio understanding models has made it feasible to evaluate such complex scenarios using LLM-as-a-Judge approaches. To bridge this gap, we introduce DRAMA-Eval, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating such systems. DRAMA-Eval utilizes structured script contexts and offers a holistic evaluation framework covering objective, local, and global aspects of generation quality, enabling the assessment of acoustic fidelity, sentence-level execution, and long-range coherence. We benchmark leading open-source and commercial models on a human?verified dataset. The results reveal critical weaknesses in long-range speaker consistency and implicit instruction following that require deep contextual understanding. To facilitate reproducible research, we release a 12-hour bilingual (Chinese-English) test set of manually corrected real-world scripts, accompanied by ground-truth audio, evaluation code, and benchmark results.

Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping academic work, yet its occupational health implications for academicians remain under-examined. The Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework offers a dual lens for understanding AI as both a performance-enhancing resource and a source of job demands, but no systematic review has applied this framework across the full spectrum of academic roles. Objective This systematic review examines how AI impacts academicians’ performance across four core domains—teaching, research, community engagement, and professional development—using the JD-R framework to understand AI's dual nature as both a resource and a demand. Methods Following PRISMA guidelines and the five-stage framework of Khan et al., 1 we systematically searched Scopus and Web of Science databases for empirical studies published between 2021 and 2025. After screening 868 records, 30 peer-reviewed journal articles met the inclusion criteria. A two-phase coding approach (deductive and inductive) was employed, with intercoder reliability (Cohen's Kappa = 0.91) indicating strong agreement. Thematic analysis was guided by the JD-R framework. Results Teaching performance dominates the literature (70%), reflecting AI's immediate impact on instructional practices. AI functions as a job resource through enhanced personalized learning, assessment automation, and administrative efficiency when supported by self-efficacy, AI literacy, and institutional resources. However, AI creates significant job demands including academic integrity management, assessment redesign, continuous upskilling, and ethical dilemmas. Professional development (27%) exhibits the most severe demand-resource imbalance, with faculty experiencing skill obsolescence anxiety, technostress, and imposter syndrome. Research performance (20%) shows a relatively balanced profile, while community engagement (7%) remains critically understudied. Identity-threatening demands—academic integrity in teaching, authorship ambiguity in research, and skill obsolescence in professional development—generate disproportionate psychological strain requiring specialized buffers. Conclusions AI's impact on academic work is inherently dualistic, with outcomes determined by the balance between available resources and demand intensity. Psychological resources, particularly self-efficacy, emerge as the most powerful enablers mediating the effectiveness of institutional and knowledge resources. The review extends JD-R theory by identifying identity-threatening demands as a distinct demand category and proposing a Resource Cascade Model wherein distal organizational resources foster proximal psychological resources. Institutions must adopt systemic, autonomy-supportive interventions addressing the full spectrum of AI's impact on academic work.

The article substantiates the structure, assessment criteria and levels of managerial competence of preschool leaders in dual in-service training. Effective leadership practices in early childhood education, personal leadership resources and theories of workplace learning were comparatively analysed. Competence was interpreted as a two-dimensional construct formed at the intersection of four practice domains and four personal resources, and criteria and indicators were defined for each domain. A four-level scale based on the Dreyfus model and a development cycle linking the training institution with the preschool organisation were proposed.

Neurological emergencies span a wide spectrum, from sudden vascular events such as ischemic stroke to acute psychiatric-neurological crises such as panic attacks. Both categories are time-sensitive and both currently rely heavily on manual clinical assessment, which limits the speed and consistency of detection. This paper presents a detailed review of six recent peer-reviewed sources (2024–2025) on artificial intelligence (AI) in neurology, and uses their combined findings to build a case for, and a design of, an integrated two-module early-detection framework: an imaging-based deep-learning pipeline for stroke triage, and a wearable-sensor-based sequence-modelling pipeline for panic/anxiety detection. The review covers foundational AI concepts (machine learning, deep learning, neural network architectures), the current clinical evidence base for stroke-imaging AI, the comparatively nascent evidence for physiological/behavioural AI in affective and psychiatric-neurological states, and the shared ethical, technical, and regulatory challenges — interpretability, bias, data privacy, and validation — that recur across every source reviewed. The paper then details a proposed system architecture, dataset and preprocessing requirements, candidate model architectures, an evaluation plan with specific metrics, expected outcomes, and a discussion of limitations and future work. The overall conclusion is that stroke-detection AI is a mature and clinically validated field that can serve as a design template for a still-emerging class of wearable, sensor-driven AI tools for detecting acute panic and anxiety states.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Issue No. 69 of Rhetoric and Communications continues the tradition of publishing research findings obtained through both traditional and contemporary methods, focusing on new and rapidly evolving fields of analysis, such as artificial intelligence, digitalization, the media ecosystem, and changes in education at the university and school levels. This issue brings together 12 scholarly articles in two sections. The first one is titled “Communication in Media and Society”, and two of the articles in this section are devoted to fact-checking, a topical issue in contemporary media and communication studies. In one article, researchers Milen Filipov and Nilufar Sulaimonova present findings related to an analysis of fact-checking activities in the media in Kazakhstan. In the second article, Tihomira Doncheva presents the results of a study on fact-checking and the use of artificial intelligence. The second area of research focuses on the media in Bulgaria. Aneta Milkova examines the legal framework, the limits of media regulation, and communication. Tanya Dimova discusses the functions of the Bulgarian National Radio, emphasizing the cultural role of the “Hristo Botev” program while taking into account changes in the digital media landscape. Alexander Blagoev presents the results of a study on social identity in communication through memes and participation in online challenges. Damyan Bumbalov clarifies, from a theoretical and methodological perspective, the scope and content of the concept of “monumental sculpture” and its communicative functions in public space. The second section includes interesting publications in which rhetoric and communication are studied in university and school settings. Faculty members from two universities in Ukraine – Mykola Chursin, Halyna Shevchenko, Tetiana Antonenko, and Tetiana Zinovieva – present the results of a timely and in-depth theoretical review related to changes in higher education resulting from technological transformations and the rapid integration of artificial intelligence into the educational process. The topic of artificial intelligence is also addressed in several other articles. Radeya Gesheva analyzes the transformations in the didactics of foreign-language literature in the era of artificial intelligence, focusing on Italian literature, for the teaching of which she provides many excellent practical examples in terms of methodology. Rhetoric is explored in new and interesting fields from a scholarly and methodological perspective: art, theater, education, and teaching in academic and school settings. Evgenia Roeva presents the findings of a study on the application of rhetoric and public speaking in education and its intersections with educational theater when working with elementary school students. Ralitsa Bezhan presents the results of a study on fundamental rhetorical canons from Aristotle to the era of artificial intelligence, contemporary theatrical performances and productions, and chatbots. Irena Shunina presents, in a captivating and compelling manner, the rhetoric of the heart and ethics in Shalva Amonashvili’s humanistic pedagogy. Boyan Zahariev highlights the specifics of pedagogical communication when using the LEGO® Serious Play® method: spatial projections and social identity as the result of field observation and a pedagogical experiment with Roma students from a neighborhood school

Purpose The accelerated transformations of the digital economy require a profound rethinking of higher education, especially in terms of preparing human capital for a future shaped by artificial intelligence (AI). The use of AI is no longer a peripheral technological option. Still, it has become a central vector in defining the skills required in the labour market, streamlining educational processes, and reshaping the relationship between learning and performance. Design/methodology/approach This paper aims to analyse, from a cross-border perspective, how AI is integrated into higher education in Romania, the Republic of Moldova and Ukraine. The investigation examines the relationships among available educational resources, AI use, AI-related skills, meta-competencies, self-reported perceived academic performance and career intentions in an emerging digital context. Findings The study uses a convergent mixed-methods design, combining survey data from 678 students with 76 semi-structured interviews with university teachers. The findings show that AI adoption is shaped by the interaction between institutional resources, actual use, AI-related skills, meta-competencies and national context. Students from Romania and the Republic of Moldova reported more frequent and varied AI use than students from Ukraine, while the Ukrainian profile reflected a more cautious pattern shaped by risk perception and contextual constraints. The results also indicate that resources and institutional support matter mainly when they translate into concrete AI use and competence development. Originality/value The study contributes empirically and contextually to comparative research on educational technology adoption by showing that AI integration in higher education depends not only on technological acceptance, but also on institutional readiness, educational equity, digital access and responsible pedagogical governance.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has transformed health sciences education, particularly in the field of clinical training.This systematic review aimed to analyze the impact of digital technologies on clinical training in health sciences education.The review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines.A comprehensive literature search was performed in three major databases: Scopus, PubMed/MEDLINE, and Web of Science.The search initially identified 498 records.After removing duplicates and applying eligibility criteria, 18 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis.The included studies examined various digital technologies applied to clinical education, including simulation-based learning systems, artificial intelligence tools, digital learning platforms, and online educational resources.Overall, the findings indicate that digital technologies significantly enhance clinical training by improving procedural skills, clinical reasoning, and student engagement.Simulation environments and virtual learning systems provide safe and controlled settings where students can practice clinical procedures without compromising patient safety.Additionally, digital educational platforms facilitate flexible learning and promote the development of digital competencies among healthcare students and professionals.Despite these benefits, challenges such as technological infrastructure limitations and the need for faculty training remain important considerations.In conclusion, digital technologies represent a valuable strategy for strengthening clinical education and preparing healthcare professionals for increasingly technology-driven healthcare systems.

Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) are diverse conditions characterised by selective dysfunction and progressive loss of neurons, glial cells, and neural networks in the brain and spinal cord. NDs pose a major global health challenge due to ageing populations and lack of cure, prompting interest in developing algorithms for early detection and biomarkers. Electroencephalography (EEG), a non-invasive and cost-effective tool, has emerged as a promising method for identifying neural signatures of NDs. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) have further enabled automated diagnosis, disease monitoring, and prognostic modelling using EEG data. This review synthesises evidence from 226 studies, mapping the current landscape of EEG-based diagnosis, prognosis, and patient stratification across various NDs. Unlike prior reviews, it provides a comprehensive overview across multiple disorders, including rare ones, and evaluates the role of ML and AI in clinical translation. We analyse research trends, EEG acquisition and preprocessing, and the development of biomarkers for disease diagnosis, prognosis, treatment monitoring, and patient stratification. Spectral power, event-related potentials, and connectivity are the main features, with support vector machines and neural networks as the primary classifiers. We review clinical trials involving EEG in NDs and highlight open-source EEG repositories to support reproducibility and data sharing. Despite promising results, challenges such as small sample sizes, methodological differences, limited model interpretability, and gaps in clinical validation remain. The review highlights the potential of EEG combined with ML/AI for early diagnosis and therapy, while outlining future directions through standardised pipelines, explainable models, and collaborative open data initiatives.

This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to evaluate the effectiveness of artificial intelligence-based therapeutic conversational agent interventions for depressive and anxiety symptoms among university students. The review focuses on parallel-group randomized controlled trials evaluating therapeutic conversational agents or chatbots designed to provide psychological treatment or therapeutic psychological support. The primary outcomes are depressive and anxiety symptoms measured using validated assessment instruments.
topics: Anxiety, Depression, Psychometrics, Treatment, Cognitive Processes

documents.abstract: The rapid development of digital technology has significantly influenced the entire design process, particularly the conceptual phase, affecting designers’ cognition and creativity. This study systematically reviewed the literature to provide a comprehensive understanding of how digital tools support design cognition in the conceptual design phase and identify future research directions. The findings indicate that individual digital tools offer various advantages, such as providing broader perspectives, facilitating rapid idea development, and enhancing motivation. However, the strength and generalizability of the evidence were constrained by limitations in participant sampling and variation in reliability and validity procedures across studies. The review identified key areas for future research, including exploring the cognitive benefits of artificial intelligence (AI) design tools with designers, applying innovative methods and analyses to understand design cognition, examining the benefits of digital tools in simulated professional design environments, and exploring distributed collaborative design settings. The study highlighted the need for further research to deepen understanding of digital tools and their application in conceptual design.

Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers learners immediate and personalized support, yet unguided interaction may encourage passive use and weaken self-regulated learning (SRL). This study examined whether question-chain prompting can support SRL in human-AI interaction. A quasi-experiment was conducted with 83 undergraduates enrolled in a television program production course. A control group used free-form questioning, whereas two experimental groups used either a progressive or a divergent question-chain strategy. Data included GenAI interaction logs, post-task reflections, metacognitive awareness measures, and course grades. This study found that both question-chain groups demonstrated significantly more learning-strategy and learning-monitoring behaviors than the control group. Reflection data further indicated differences in students’ approaches to human-AI collaboration, although these differences should be interpreted cautiously because the reflection prompts differed by condition. Moreover, both experimental groups scored significantly higher than the control group on knowledge of cognition, regulation of cognition, and academic achievement. No significant differences were found between the progressive and divergent question-chain approaches. The findings suggest that question-chain prompting, implemented as an instructional package of specific, sequenced, and required questions, can promote more active engagement during human-AI interaction and support metacognitive development and learning performance. Question chains offer a practical approach for guiding students’ use of GenAI in educational settings.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Omni-modal large language models (Omni-LLMs) can jointly process a broad range of modalities, such as text, audio, and video, enabling stronger multimodal understanding and reasoning capabilities, but often at substantial inference cost. We observe that the benefit of additional modalities varies across queries, indicating that a fixed modality configuration can be inefficient. Motivated by this, we study query-wise modality selection, which keeps the underlying Omni-LLM fixed while adaptively selecting which modalities to provide for each query. We formulate the problem as an accuracy-cost optimization problem and develop a cost-sensitive learning approach for modality selection. We evaluate our approach on WorldSense using Qwen2.5-Omni and Qwen3-Omni under three inference-cost measures: input tokens, latency, and monetary cost. Across both models, query-wise modality selection consistently improves the accuracy-cost trade-off and can even outperform the standard setting in which all available modalities are provided to the Omni-LLM. For Qwen2.5-Omni, our cost-sensitive approach matches or exceeds this full-modality accuracy while requiring only approximately 41% of the input tokens, 39% of the latency, and 61% of the monetary cost.

Background. Pedagogical innovation is one of the main challenges facing higher education in the twenty-first century, as digital transformation now shapes every mode of instruction and calls into question the way students build knowledge. Objective. To develop an emerging pedagogical model that strengthens knowledge and learning among undergraduate students, drawing on the experiences of students, faculty, and administrators across different educational modes. Methods. A qualitative study was conducted under the interpretive-critical paradigm using a grounded theory design. A total of 221 participants from three Colombian institutions representing on-campus, military on-campus, and online modes were selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews, supported by document analysis of reports issued by the Colombian Ministry of National Education and by observational research. The analysis involved open, axial, and selective coding, source triangulation, and categorical convergence analysis. Results. Eight emerging categories were identified: pedagogical innovation as the organizing axis, participation and dialogue, reflective assessment, critical thinking, faculty development, educational equity, meaningful learning, and the pedagogical use of artificial intelligence and ICT. The three groups agreed that changing educational practice depends not on adopting technology or making isolated methodological changes, but on aligning pedagogy, didactics, teaching strategies, and the instructional context. Conclusions. The convergence of these categories gives rise to the Pedagogical Model of Critical Innovation, an emerging theoretical construct that offers a conceptual reference for updating institutional education projects, pedagogical models, and curriculum designs across the different modes of higher education.

Artificial intelligence is reshaping how political campaigns are produced and circulated. In Nigeria, parties, candidates, and supporters now rely heavily on digital tools to create adverts, images, and voice messages, yet little is known about how ordinary electorates in South-South Nigeria read such content. This exploratory study therefore examined how registered voters in South-South Nigeria distinguish AI-generated from human-created campaign messages, explain their trust or distrust in them, and describe their emotional responses and possible voting intentions ahead of the 2027 elections. A qualitative exploratory design was used. Nineteen registered voters aged 18–40 who actively use social media were purposively selected for maximum variation. Data were collected through online semi-structured interviews using six campaign messages, along with observation notes, and analysed with reflexive thematic analysis. Participants identified AI mainly through unnatural movement, implausible settings and contextual inconsistencies. Human-created messages were generally trusted more, although emotionally relevant AI content could also appear credible. Emotional reactions included humour, hope, confusion and worry, but these rarely translated directly into voting intention. Within this sample, recognition, trust and voting responses depended on realism, relevance, prior knowledge and candidate credibility. As exploratory findings, these are not statistically generalisable but offer propositions for larger, representative studies.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Arthritis is one of the leading causes of chronic pain, disability, and reduced quality of life worldwide, affecting millions of individuals through progressive joint inflammation, cartilage degeneration, and bone destruction.Although conventional therapies, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), glucocorticoids, disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs), biologics, and Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors, effectively alleviate symptoms and delay disease progression, their long-term use is frequently associated with adverse effects, high treatment costs, and incomplete disease remission.Consequently, phytotherapy has emerged as a promising complementary and alternative therapeutic strategy owing to its multitarget pharmacological actions and comparatively favorable safety profile.This review comprehensively summarizes the current knowledge on the pathophysiology of arthritis, emphasizing inflammatory cytokines, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and major intracellular signaling pathways, including NF-κB, MAPK, JAK/STAT, PI3K/Akt, NLRP3 inflammasome, COX-2, and 5-lipoxygenase.Particular attention is given to bioactive phytoconstituents such as curcumin, resveratrol, quercetin, kaempferol, luteolin, apigenin, catechins, boswellic acids, thymoquinone, berberine, and other polyphenols, flavonoids, terpenoids, alkaloids, saponins, tannins, and glycosides.Furthermore, the review compiles experimental pharmacological evidence from in vitro and in vivo studies, summarizes medicinal plants with established anti-arthritic activity, and highlights their molecular targets and mechanisms of action.Emerging advances in nanotechnology-based phytopharmaceuticals, molecular docking, network pharmacology, omics technologies, and artificial intelligence are also discussed as future directions for improving the efficacy, bioavailability, and precision of plant-derived therapeutics.Collectively, the available evidence indicates that phytochemicals exert anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, immunomodulatory, and chondroprotective effects through simultaneous modulation of multiple molecular pathways.However, further standardization, pharmacokinetic evaluation, and well-designed multicenter clinical trials are required to facilitate their successful translation into evidence-based clinical practice.This review provides an integrated scientific framework for researchers and clinicians involved in the development of safer, multitarget, and effective phytotherapeutic interventions for arthritis management.

The United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), adopted in 2015, offer a global guide to eliminate poverty, safeguard the planet, and promote prosperity by 2030. Higher education institutions (HEIs) are uniquely well placed as a knowledge centre to hasten the pace of learning by performing their main roles, such as academia (teaching and learning), administration (governance and operation), and innovation and research. The current study aims to find ways Artificial Intelligence (AI) can boost sustainability and what challenges and chances it brings in managing and promoting sustainability. The results show that AI can optimize resources by using models that predict how to cut down on energy use, improve how people move around campus, and reduce waste. In teaching, AI makes things more sustainable by offering personalized learning, digital tutoring, instant feedback, and immersive experiences to enhance student motivation and engagement. In research, AI can make a significant impact by making it easier to analyze big datasets on environmental, social, and economic topics. The study finds that responsible and fair AI implementation in academia, administration, and research is necessary to help HEIs close SDG gaps. Three major recommendations are: ethical AI governance and faculty development, AI-optimized sustainable campus operation, and interdisciplinary AI-driven research hubs. In recent years, the demand for strategic adoption of AI in higher education has increased, particularly to fulfill SDGs and ensure that all people enjoy peace and prosperity by 2030. This study encourages institutions to establish funded AI hubs that foster cross-disciplinary research and international collaborations to produce evidence-based solutions to various SDGs, such as health (SDG 3), clean energy (SDG 7), and biodiversity (SDG 15).

Purpose This study aims to explore how personalized services provided by pre-consultation chatbots influence patients' intentions to self-disclose and the boundary conditions of this effect. Drawing on the Communication Privacy Management Theory, it identifies AI interactive trust as a mediator and examines how disease sensitivity moderates this mechanism. Design/methodology/approach Three scenario experiments and a field survey were conducted to test hypotheses. Experiments 1 and 2 were between-subjects experiments that manipulated pre-consultation chatbot service personalization (low vs. high) in different disease contexts. Experiment 3 employed a 2 (service personalization: low vs. high) × 2 (disease type: low- vs. high-sensitivity) between-subjects design. Survey 4 reconfirmed all hypotheses. Findings Service personalization increased patients' willingness to self-disclose by enhancing AI interactive trust, but only for low-sensitivity diseases. For high-sensitivity conditions, this trust-based effect weakens or even disappears. Originality/value By uncovering the central role of relationship quality in human-AI interactions, this study delivers novel theoretical insights, distinct from prior benefit-risk frameworks, into the internal mechanisms by which AI service personalization shapes users' willingness to self-disclose, extending existing research on the mechanisms of personalized AI services.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Intelligent Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) has a pivotal place in sarcasm detection, given that sarcastic utterances may have an intended meaning that is not in the literal meaning of the spoken words. Sarcasm is also difficult to spot correctly since it varies not only in text but also in voice and other visual indicators like facial expression and body language. Unimodal sarcasm detection methods are generally limited by contextual ambiguity, the insensitivity of contextual paralinguistic cues, and decreased performance in situations where one modality is noisy or incomplete. These problems may cause unpredictable results and inadequate functionality in the real conversational context. To overcome these shortcomings, for sarcasm detection, we suggest an approach with different modalities which uses multi-modal cues like audio, video as well as text to provide complementary information from various communication channels. In the case of textual representation, the RoBERTa architecture was used to elicit deep contextual and semantic features of dialog transcripts. The HuBERT architecture was used to model acoustic features and is effective at representing speech representations in terms of prosodic and tonal variation based on sarcastic speech. Simultaneously, the ViViT architecture was used to process visual data and identify both spatial and temporal patterns of facial expressions and gestures in videos. Modality-specific feature representations are then combined with a Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) based fusion strategy which decides best-found modality weights by minimizing classification loss. The fused representation is then optimized and then through the two-layer fully connected classifier to classify sarcasm. The suggested framework was evaluated with the publicly available MUStARD dataset. The model displayed an accuracy of 94% and the recall, precision and weighted F1-score were all equal to 0.94. Comparative evaluation also compared the proposed PSO-Multimodal Fusion Model with the unimodal models and also with the traditional multimodal fusion models such as attention-based model, Graph-based model, Generative Approach, LLM/Modeling-based model, and contrastive learning approach, and showed that the proposed multimodal fusion framework yields the highest weighted F1-score among the evaluated approaches. Experimental outcomes prove that the multimodal fusion methodology based on optimization enhances the performance of sarcasm detection in contrast to the unimodal and traditional fusion techniques, which indicate its efficiency in practical use in conversational AI.

Single-Pilot Operations (SPO) in commercial aviation raise critical safety challenges in complex, time-pressured situations where human expertise is paramount. This study investigates how AI-based Human-Autonomy Teaming (HAT) can support pilot decision-making under high workload, compromised situational awareness, and time pressure. In a high-fidelity Airbus A320 simulator, 22 airline pilots performed a fuel- and time-constrained approach scenario designed to challenge HAT’s operational effectiveness under four conditions: no assistance, on-demand AI, proactive AI, and proactive explainable AI. Workload (NASA-TLX) remained high across conditions, yet decision-making differed markedly. Without assistance, only 20% chose the safest landing option; with on-demand AI, 40%; and with proactive AI (both versions), 100%. Explainable AI yielded the highest scenario comprehension (75%), matching two-crew baseline performance. Proactive systems increased decision and SA related interactions, fostering a collaborative dynamic akin to traditional crew resource management. Thus, the results demonstrate that, in the context of SPO, proactive and explainable AI was associated with crew-level decision performance within the experimental scenario without adding cognitive load. Beyond the aeronautical domain, our results are of interest for the design of cognitive support systems for high-risk domains where teams composed of humans and AI must adapt in real time.

Teachers' limited competence in utilizing Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based digital media has hindered the effective implementation of innovative teaching practices and environmental projects. This community service program aimed to enhance teachers' knowledge and skills in developing AI-based instructional media. The program was conducted at State Senior High School 1 Koto Kampar Hulu and involved 29 teachers through educational seminars, workshops, hands-on practice, and mentoring using Canva AI, Gemini AI, and NotebookLM. Program effectiveness was evaluated using pretest-posttest assessments, N-Gain analysis, instructional media product evaluation, and participant satisfaction questionnaires. The results showed that the participants' mean score increased from 47.0 to 78.9, with an N-Gain score of 0.6, indicating a moderate level of improvement. All participants (100%) demonstrated increased knowledge following the training. Furthermore, every participant successfully developed at least one AI-based instructional medium, such as a poster or infographic, that was ready for implementation in classroom instruction and environmental projects. These findings indicate that the training effectively enhanced teachers' digital competencies and their ability to integrate AI technologies into teaching and learning practices

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Tool-using language model agents rely on environmental facts to decide whether an action is permitted. When a tool response omits a safety-relevant fact, an agent may carry out a prohibited action even though the user request is benign and every returned statement is true. We introduce \bench{}, an executable benchmark for evaluating unsafe execution, safety boundaries, and evidence recovery in LLM agents under missing evidence. It contains 300 matched unsafe/safe task pairs across six domains. By systematically suppressing critical facts, the benchmark measures unsafe execution under critical evidence omission and determines the minimum observed failure cardinality, including failures with full evidence and cases with no observed failure after exhaustive testing. An independent audit tool tests whether agents seek missing facts and then withhold prohibited actions while completing permissible tasks. The benchmark reveals substantial variation across the ten models in omission robustness, evidence acquisition, and appropriate action. Resistance to missing evidence does not necessarily translate into useful recovery. Recovery access reduces unsafe execution for all ten models, but agents differ in whether they actively obtain the missing facts and use them to act appropriately in both worlds.

documents.abstract: Women constitute a substantial share of the agricultural labor force in Africa, yet the tools and machinery available to them are mostly designed based on male anthropometric norms; this imposes avoidable musculoskeletal risk and drudgery. This study evaluated the ergonomic compatibility of four commonly used farm implements, a traditional hoe, a manually operated groundnut harvester, a knapsack sprayer, and a cassava frying/garri-processing station. It considered the anthropometric and postural needs of women farm operators, and tested a set of dimensional optimizations intended to reduce musculoskeletal risk. One hundred and fifty (150) women farm operators aged 20–55 years in south-western Nigeria were anthropometrically measured across sixteen body dimensions, and postural risk during machine operation was assessed using the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) and Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) methods, complemented by the Standardized Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ) and an Overall Discomfort Rating (ODR, Borg CR-10 scale). Anthropometric analysis showed that there is a substantial mismatch between machine dimensions and the accommodating range of females; between 24% and 88% of operators fell outside the recommended fit envelope for individual interface parameters. Based on dimensional optimization of handle height, grip diameter, working height, and load distribution, mean REBA scores fell from 7.7 ± 1.0 to 4.4 ± 0.7, and mean RULA scores fell from 6.1 ± 0.9 to 3.8 ± 0.6 in a one-way ANOVA and paired t-test, p < 0.00. Musculoskeletal discomfort that had prevailed for 12 months fell across all nine body regions assessed by the NMQ. It was most notable in the lower back from 74% to 35%, shoulders from 69% to 31%, and wrists/hands from 61% to 22%. The results showed that the redesign of machine operator interfaces can measurably reduce musculoskeletal risk and drudgery among women farmers. The study proposes a replicable ergonomic optimization protocol for extension and manufacturing use.

Technical, social, avant-garde, global, and cognitive pressures are driving the adoption of new technologies characterized by constant updates and automation most notably generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and autonomous agents. While the stated intention is to augment and enhance human capabilities regarding complex challenges, skills, and critical thinking rather than replacing them recent empirical evidence suggests the actual trend is moving in the opposite direction, to the detriment of consumers. This study analyzes the flaws and risks stemming from the use and misuse of these cutting-edge technologies, aiming to propose intervention frameworks before they become irreversibly entrenched in a fragile structure within the technology adoption cycle. It explores phenomena such as the atrophy of technical skills, the productivity paradox, cognitive offloading, over-reliance on automated systems, and the irony of automation, drawing on evidence from randomized controlled trials and large-scale surveys conducted between 2025 and 2026. This analysis examines the critical failures and systemic risks of these cutting-edge technologies, aiming to propose regulatory and operational intervention frameworks before their negative effects become irreversibly embedded in the labor market and social fabric. Identifying these risk vectors early allows for the design of guidelines that restore human control, ensuring technology acts as a genuine complement rather than an agent of cognitive and professional erosion. Furthermore, there is high demand for courses, diploma programs, and workshops focused on critical thinking, reflecting a growing awareness of the need to pursue them.

documents.abstract: On 25 May 2026, Pope Leo XIV's Magnifica Humanitas became the first papal encyclical on artificial intelligence, declaring that lethal decisions cannot be entrusted to artificial systems and calling for a shared international framework to govern military AI. It states these principles but does not operationalise them. This article develops that operational framework. Applying Catholic social doctrine (human dignity and agency, subsidiarity, prudence, intentionality, the common good, and the protection of noncombatants) to military AI, it translates the encyclical's commitments into concrete requirements for autonomous weapons, targeting systems, and alliance interoperability. It grounds the argument in the nuclear precedent, where Catholic ethics shaped doctrine as it formed, and more briefly in chemical and biological weapons prohibition. Engaging just war theory, NATO's Principles of Responsible Use, recent military wargaming, and a leading AI provider's treatment of a catastrophic strike as consistent with its self-declared “red lines,” it shows where Catholic ethics is more demanding than procedural compliance. It then proposes institutional mechanisms: a tiered deliberation framework, proportionality dossiers, ethics review boards, and NATO-level coordination. Building ethical architecture before deployment, the article argues, serves strategic as well as moral interests.

documents.abstract: Ethnic diversity significantly influences anaesthetic pharmacology and perioperative outcomes through complex interactions between genetic, physiological, environmental and social determinants of health. There is increasing evidence suggesting that different ethnic populations demonstrate variability in anaesthetic drug metabolism, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, pain perception and recovery characteristics. Pharmacogenomic variations in cytochrome P450 enzymes contribute to clinically significant differences in opioid metabolism, sedative and analgesic response, and postoperative recovery. In addition, epigenetic influences, such as DNA methylation and histone modification, may further affect pain modulation, opioid responsiveness and susceptibility to perioperative neurocognitive effects. Ethnic disparities in perioperative care extend beyond biological variability, with minority populations demonstrating differences in access to regional anaesthesia, obstetric anaesthesia services, perioperative pain management and paediatric perioperative care. Various factors, like structural inequalities, communication barriers, implicit bias and unequal healthcare, contribute to these disparities. Advances in pharmacogenomics, artificial intelligence and precision perioperative medicine may lead to more individualized anaesthetic management in the future. However, important challenges, such as limited representation of diverse populations in research, and limited understanding of gene – environment interactions, need to be addressed. A better understanding of ethnic variability in anaesthetic pharmacology may improve anaesthetic safety, optimize perioperative drug dosing and selection, and promote equitable perioperative care across diverse patient populations.

BackgroundNail technicians face significant risks of musculoskeletal disorders due to ergonomic challenges. Nail technicians' working conditions and health risks can be evaluated to develop strategies that enhance their well-being.ObjectiveThis study assesses the working conditions, occupational symptoms, and potential risk factors for musculoskeletal disorders among nail technicians.MethodsThis cross-sectional study involved 35 female nail technicians. Data were collected through interviews, pain assessments, occupational details, the Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire, and the Quick Exposure Check (QEC) for ergonomic risks.ResultsA significant proportion of technicians reported respiratory issues (37.1%), skin problems (14.2%), and musculoskeletal pain, particularly in the neck (51%), upper back (57%), and lower back (31%). QEC levels showed that back static positions and neck and wrist/hand exposures were in the "very high risk" category, while shoulder/arm exposures were classified as "high risk". Neck and static back QEC scores were significantly correlated with weekly working hours and years of experience (r = 0.828, p < 0.001), and reported pain was strongly linked to QEC risk scores for these areas (r = 0.944, p < 0.001).ConclusionsThe findings regarding nail technicians' working conditions and health risks underscore the necessity for ergonomic training and workplace modifications to mitigate these risks. Early intervention is essential to prevent chronic work-related disorders and improve technicians' health and quality of life.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Generative AI democratizes entrepreneurship by lowering barriers to ideation, creating an environment of abundance. Yet while AI produces speed, scale, and local autonomy, these benefits may come at hidden costs to output quality. Using illustrative vignettes to ground and elaborate, we particularly identify explainability, traceability, and generalizability as costs of abundance. As AI separates observable output from the expertise traditionally required to produce it, the entrepreneur's attention to evaluation becomes the scarce resource. We identify three trade‐offs and their interdependencies for entrepreneurs: speed‐to‐understanding, scale‐to‐oversight, and local autonomy‐to‐system‐wide relevance. Implications for human accountability of AI systems and governance (organizational design) challenges for entrepreneurs are discussed. Managerial Summary AI allows entrepreneurial firms to produce ideas and other outputs faster and at greater scale than ever before. As AI separates output from the expertise traditionally gained while creating it, the scarce resource shifts from generation to evaluation. This creates new managerial tensions: speed versus understanding, scale versus oversight, and local autonomy versus system‐wide relevance. These tensions help explain concerns about AI “going rogue”: simply keeping a human in the loop is not enough if the human expertise no longer includes the ability to understand, trace, question, and override the system. Entrepreneurs are challenged to design organizations that preserve meaningful human expertise and accountability.
